title: Case Report: Distal ureteral obstruction decades after presumed intrauterine device removal in a woman with uterus didelphys.
abstract: Background An ectopic intrauterine device (IUD) can rarely cause ureteral obstruction and hydroureteronephrosis. Diagnosis may be delayed when a prior removal procedure is believed to have been complete. Case presentation A 48-year-old woman presented with a 1-year history of right flank pain and urinary frequency after repeated treatment for presumed urinary tract infection and possible genitourinary tuberculosis without sustained improvement. More than 20 years earlier, an IUD had been inserted before uterus didelphys was recognized. Two to three years later, an unintended pregnancy led to recognition of the duplicated uterine anatomy, induced abortion, and an IUD removal procedure. The original records were unavailable, so device location and intact retrieval at that time could not be verified. Multimodality imaging at the index admission showed severe right hydroureteronephrosis, focal distal ureteral narrowing, and an ectopic metallic IUD outside both uterine cavities; cystoscopy was unremarkable. Open ureteral exploration and reconstruction identified an intact IUD with an attached calculus externally compressing an approximately 1-cm fixed distal ureteral stricture without entering the ureteral lumen. The narrowing persisted after device removal, requiring segmental ureteral resection and anastomosis over a double-J stent. Histopathology of the resected ureter showed chronic inflammatory changes without tuberculous changes. The stent was removed 2 months postoperatively. At 6 months after surgery, computed tomography showed marked decompression of the right collecting system and no residual pelvic metallic device; serum creatinine remained normal. Conclusion A history of IUD removal should not be treated as proof of device absence when intact retrieval is undocumented. In otherwise unexplained unilateral ureteral obstruction, a remote IUD history should prompt review of prior device localization and targeted pelvic imaging, particularly when historical records are unavailable or duplicated uterine anatomy complicates localization. A fixed stricture may require reconstruction even after the ectopic device is removed.

title: EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection and immediate intraoperative bleeding during endoscopic mucosal resection: a retrospective cohort study (with video).
abstract: Objective To investigate whether endoscopic ultrasound (EUS)-guided targeted epinephrine injection is associated with a lower rate of bleeding during endoscopic mucosal resection (EMR). Methods This retrospective cohort study enrolled consecutive patients undergoing EMR for gastrointestinal lesions ≥1 cm with an EUS-detectable feeding vessel at Zhengzhou Central Hospital between January 2025 and March 2026. Patients were non-randomly assigned to EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection (1:20,000) or EUS assessment followed by conventional submucosal saline injection. The primary outcome was immediate intraoperative bleeding; secondary outcomes included delayed bleeding, procedure time, hospital stay, en bloc resection rate, and adverse events. Multivariable logistic regression was performed, with Firth regression and propensity-score (PSM and IPTW) sensitivity analyses to address confounding. Results Among 84 patients (injection group, n = 31; control group, n = 53), immediate intraoperative bleeding occurred in 0% versus 24.5% ( P = 0.002). Two delayed bleeding cases (3.8%) occurred in the control group only. No between-group differences were observed in procedure time, hospital stay, or adverse events; the en bloc resection rate was 100% in both groups. EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection was associated with reduced odds of intraoperative bleeding (OR = 0.112, 95% CI 0.028-0.443, P = 0.002), consistent across Firth regression, PSM, and IPTW analyses. Conclusion EUS-guided targeted epinephrine injection was associated with lower immediate intraoperative bleeding during EMR without prolonging procedure time or hospital stay. These hypothesis-generating findings require confirmation in prospective randomized studies.

title: Case Report: Durable, well-tolerated complete response to epcoritamab plus pirtobrutinib in Richter transformation relapsing after CD19 CAR T-cell therapy.
abstract: Richter transformation (RT) that relapses after CD19-directed chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy has no established therapy and carries a dismal prognosis. We report an 84-year-old man with multiply relapsed, biopsy-proven diffuse large B-cell lymphoma-type RT and a high-risk MYC/BCL2 double-expressor phenotype who developed systemic relapse, with extensive osteolytic bone disease, after lisocabtagene maraleucel. Three cycles of atezolizumab produced no objective benefit. Treatment with epcoritamab, a CD3xCD20 bispecific antibody, plus pirtobrutinib, a non-covalent Bruton tyrosine kinase inhibitor, produced complete nodal metabolic resolution within 3 months that deepened to a complete metabolic response (Deauville score 2) by 10 treatment cycles, with resolution of two interim osteolytic lesions whose transient nature illustrates the interpretive challenges of PET/CT response assessment after cellular and T-cell-engaging therapies. The chemotherapy-free regimen was well tolerated at age 84, with no cytokine release syndrome, no neurotoxicity, and no cytopenias; the only toxicity was mild, reversible dexamethasone-related myopathy. The patient remains in ongoing clinical remission after approximately 10 months of therapy. This case extends the reported experience with epcoritamab plus pirtobrutinib specifically to the post-CAR T-cell relapse setting and suggests that this chemotherapy-free doublet may warrant consideration as a salvage strategy for older or frail patients with RT who are unfit for further cytotoxic therapy.

title: MammoDiff: weakly supervised mammographic anomaly detection via classifier-guided denoising diffusion models-a real-world clinical study on the KHCC mammography cohort.
abstract: Introduction Early detection of malignant mammographic lesions is a critical clinical challenge, particularly where large annotated datasets are unavailable. Supervised deep learning achieves near-radiologist performance but requires large datasets with reliable labels and pixel/ROI annotations. Weakly supervised anomaly detection, requiring only image-level binary labels, offers an annotation-efficient alternative, yet prior GAN- and autoencoder-based methods have struggled to preserve fine anatomical detail in the mammographic domain. Methods We present MammoDiff, to our knowledge the first application of classifier-guided denoising diffusion models to weakly supervised mammographic anomaly detection, trained and evaluated on 3,013 mammograms from 806 patients at King Hussein Cancer Center (KHCC), Jordan. MammoDiff encodes input anatomy through deterministic DDIM noise encoding and reconstructs a counterfactual healthy image guided by the gradient signal of a noise-conditioned binary classifier. The anomaly map is the pixel-wise absolute difference between input and reconstruction, and the image-level score is obtained by spatial mean pooling. A 3 × 3 ablation over noise level L ∈ {250, 500, 750} and gradient scale s ∈ {50, 100, 200} was performed on the validation set. Results The optimal configuration ( L = 750, s = 50) achieved AUROC = 0.7246 [95% CI: 0.6685, 0.7825] on the held-out test set ( n = 304), compared with a simplified PatchCore-style baseline (AUROC = 0.6634) and a supervised ResNet-50 reference (AUROC = 0.8100), without pixel-level annotation. The proposed Healthy-Shift Index (HSI) was positive for 94.8% of malignant and 87.4% of normal cases, so it is the separation between the class distributions rather than the sign of the index that carries information. Discussion This performance is not clinically deployable: at the Youden-optimal threshold the sensitivity is 0.6013, meaning that 61 of 153 malignant cases are missed, well below the approximately 87% targeted by FDA-cleared triage devices, and the study is single-centre without external validation. MammoDiff is therefore presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and a reproducible baseline for future work, not as a screening or triage tool..

The proposed Healthy-Shift Index (HSI) was positive for 94.8% of malignant and 87.4% of normal cases, so it is the separation between the class distributions rather than the sign of the index that carries information.

This performance is not clinically deployable: at the Youden-optimal threshold the sensitivity is 0.6013, meaning that 61 of 153 malignant cases are missed, well below the approximately 87% targeted by FDA-cleared triage devices, and the study is single-centre without external validation. MammoDiff is therefore presented as a methodological proof-of-concept and a reproducible baseline for future work, not as a screening or triage tool..

title: A technical review of dynamic brain functional imaging combined with EEG spectral parameters in the screening of early-stage brain injury.
abstract: Background Early-stage brain injury encompasses subtypes such as mild traumatic brain injury (mTBI), silent stroke and subclinical brain injury. It is characterised by negative imaging findings, subtle symptoms and a high risk of long-term neurological deficits, presenting a key challenge in the early screening and prevention of neurological diseases. Traditional imaging techniques, such as structural Magnetic Resonance Imaging (MRI) and Computed Tomography (CT), can only identify organic morphological lesions. Their detection rate for early micro-injuries at the level of neuronal electrophysiology and brain network function is extremely low. Consequently, these techniques struggle to meet the clinical needs for early screening, assessment, and intervention. Methods Electroencephalography (EEG) spectral changes (including conventional spectral slowing and 1/f aperiodic abnormalities) and large-scale dynamic neural network disruption across the entire brain are core pathological features of early brain functional damage; they may serve as indirect correlates of microscopic pathological changes such as an imbalance in neuronal excitation-inhibition and abnormalities in the efficiency of brain information transmission. Based on this, this paper proposes a Dynamic-Spectral Coupling (DSC) framework, which proposes spectral abnormalities as a potential upstream mechanism associated with network reorganisation. Within this framework, this narrative review summarizes dynamic functional magnetic resonance imaging (dynamic fMRI), EEG spectral analysis and multimodal fusion technologies, with a particular focus on elucidating the coupling mechanisms between EEG periodic and 1/f aperiodic spectral parameters and dynamic brain network indicators. Results The review outlines the screening value and application advantages of multimodal fusion technologies in mTBI, occult cerebrovascular injury and subclinical brain injury. Furthermore, the paper summarises the current limitations of these technologies in terms of clinical translation, methodology and database development. Conclusions Taking into account the clinical needs of neurorehabilitation, it proposes future development directions, including the development of lightweight devices, AI-assisted diagnosis, the establishment of standardised analytical systems and the translation of precision rehabilitation. The aim is to provide technical guidance and theoretical support for screening, risk stratification and rehabilitation planning in early-stage brain injury, while acknowledging that clinical utility remains to be established.

title: Serum GDF15 as a potential biomarker for treatment response and survival in patients with resectable locally advanced gastric cancer undergoing neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
abstract: Background Patients with locally advanced gastric cancer (LAGC) typically require neoadjuvant chemotherapy (NAC) to reduce tumor burden and improve surgical resectability. However, treatment responses to NAC vary substantially among individuals. This study investigated the potential value of baseline serum growth differentiation factor 15 (GDF15) for identifying patients at risk of poor treatment response and unfavorable survival outcomes among patients with LAGC receiving NAC. Methods We retrospectively identified 318 eligible patients with LAGC who received NAC and enrolled 30 healthy controls. Serum GDF15 levels were measured by ELISA. In the unmatched cohort, the median baseline serum GDF15 concentration (2,147.3 pg/mL), determined before PSM, was used as a fixed cutoff to define the GDF15-L and GDF15-H groups (n = 159 each). After 1:1 PSM, 256 patients (n = 128 per group) were included in the matched analyses. Comparative analyses included baseline characteristics, CT images, preoperative endoscopic biopsy specimens and postoperative pathological features. Survival outcomes (OS and DFS) were assessed via Kaplan-Meier analysis. Multivariate Cox regression identified prognostic factors, and a prognostic nomogram was constructed. Results High GDF15 expression correlated with advanced age (P = 0.045), poor tumor differentiation (P = 0.040), and elevated serum CA72-4 (P = 0.028). The GDF15-L group demonstrated superior median OS (58.1 vs. 54.0 months, P = 0.031) and DFS (47.1 vs. 26.9 months, P = 0.002) compared to GDF15-H counterparts. Preoperative endoscopic biopsy demonstrated a positive correlation between tissue GDF15 expression and serum GDF15 levels, while post-NAC imaging indicated greater tumor regression in the GDF15-L group. The GDF15-L group exhibited a higher pathological complete response (pCR) rate in postoperative pathological features (P < 0.001) while the GDF15-H group exhibited increased positive lymph nodes (P = 0.018) and a higher incidence of newly detected distant metastasis during or after NAC (P = 0.024). Multivariate analysis identified high GDF15 expression (P = 0.021) and high CAP degree (P = 0.022) as independent risk factors for OS, with younger age being protective (P = 0.016). Based on these factors, a prognostic nomogram was constructed to predict 1-year, 3-year, and 5-year OS and DFS. Conclusion Low baseline serum GDF15 levels were associated with favorable radiological and pathological responses and prolonged survival in patients with LAGC receiving NAC. Baseline serum GDF15 may help identify patients at increased risk of poor response and unfavorable prognosis and may therefore serve as a potential biomarker for pretreatment risk stratification. However, because all patients received NAC, these findings do not establish that GDF15 predicts differential benefit from NAC, and prospective validation is required.

title: Explainable machine learning integrating CT-derived intratumoral heterogeneity for histological subtype prediction in pure ground-glass lung adenocarcinoma: multicenter validation and transcriptomic characterization.
abstract: Background Preoperative differentiation of lepidic-predominant adenocarcinoma from other histological subtypes in lung adenocarcinoma presenting as pure ground-glass nodules remains challenging. We evaluated whether a CT-derived intratumoral heterogeneity score provides complementary predictive and biological information beyond routine clinical and CT features. Methods This retrospective multicenter study included 533 patients, divided into a training cohort (n = 373) and a held-out validation cohort (n = 160). Twelve supervised algorithms were compared exclusively within the training cohort using stratified five-fold cross-validation and grid-search optimization; predictors, hyperparameters, and the decision threshold were locked before the held-out cohort was evaluated once. Incremental value of the ITH score and leave-one-center-out internal-external validation were additionally assessed. Segmentation reproducibility was evaluated in 100 lesions. An independent radiogenomic cohort of 43 pathological Tis/T1 lung adenocarcinomas was analyzed by differential-expression and Hallmark gene-set enrichment analyses after median ITH-score stratification. Results XGBoost achieved the highest training-set cross-validation AUC (0.908 ± 0.021) and was selected before held-out evaluation. In the validation cohort, the AUC was 0.919 (95% CI, 0.870-0.968), with accuracy 0.850, precision 0.857, sensitivity 0.545, specificity 0.966, and Brier score 0.098. Adding the ITH score to clinical and CT features increased AUC from 0.867 to 0.919 (ΔAUC = 0.052; DeLong P = 0.012), increased PR-AUC from 0.731 to 0.824, and reduced Brier score from 0.126 to 0.098. Leave-one-center-out AUCs ranged from 0.824 to 0.882. The ITH score showed good-to-excellent repeat-segmentation reproducibility. In the radiogenomic cohort, a high ITH score was associated with coordinated enrichment of G2M checkpoint (NES = 1.86, FDR <0.001), E2F targets (NES = 1.86, FDR <0.001), and epithelial-mesenchymal transition (NES = 1.55, FDR = 0.001). Conclusion CT-derived ITH provided incremental information for histological subtype prediction and was associated with proliferation-, cell-cycle-, and EMT-related transcriptional programs. The moderate sensitivity at the prespecified operating point and the retrospective design warrant prospective external validation before clinical implementation.

title: Heterogeneous progression of AT(N) biomarkers in data-driven subtypes of Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Background Alzheimer's disease (AD) exhibits substantial heterogeneity in brain atrophy patterns and progression rates. Data-driven subtyping based on the Subtype and Stage Inference (SuStaIn) model has identified distinct MRI-derived subtypes, but the longitudinal dynamics of these subtypes within the AT(N) framework remain unknown. Methods This study included 1,576 participants from the Alzheimer's Disease Neuroimaging Initiative (ADNI) with at least two visits. SuStaIn was applied to volumetric measurements of 11 brain regions to identify imaging-based subtypes. Within each subtype, we fitted a Bayesian latent time longitudinal joint mixed-effects model incorporating six biomarkers: amyloid PET (A), CSF p-tau (T), hippocampal volume, cingulate volume, thalamic volume (N), and ADAS-Cog13 (X), with APOE ε4 as a covariate. Results The three subtypes exhibited distinctly different longitudinal patterns. Subtype 1 showed early elevation of amyloid, followed by a sharp decline in hippocampal volume, which was tightly coupled with cognitive deterioration. Subtype 2 featured early involvement of cortical regions such as the cingulate cortex, with hippocampal changes occurring at a similar timing to Subtype 1 but accompanied by earlier cortical and thalamic involvement. Subtype 3 exhibited early rapid hippocampal atrophy that later plateaued, and demonstrated the strongest hippocampus-cognition coupling. The association of APOE ε4 with biomarker trajectories was subtype-dependent: its effect estimates were largest for amyloid and p-tau in Subtype 1, whereas in Subtype 3 the effect estimates were significant for nearly all biomarkers, with the largest estimate for cognition. Conclusion This study demonstrates that AD subtypes defined by spatial atrophy patterns also differ fundamentally in temporal biomarker dynamics and APOE ε4 association, supporting subtype-stratified modeling of disease progression.

title: The ipsilesional DTI-ALPS index provides modest incremental prognostic value beyond clinical models for 90-day outcome in patients with acute MCA occlusion treated with intravenous thrombolysis: a prospective exploratory cohort study.
abstract: Background and purpose Impaired perivascular fluid dynamics may contribute to secondary brain injury after acute ischemic stroke, yet its prognostic relevance remains uncertain. We investigated whether the Diffusion Tensor Image Analysis along the Perivascular Space (ALPS) index-a quantitative MRI marker of perivascular fluid dynamics-provides incremental predictive value for long-term functional outcomes in patients with acute middle cerebral artery occlusion (MCAO) treated with intravenous thrombolysis. Methods In this prospective observational cohort study, 128 patients underwent multimodal brain MRI within 24 h of admission, and the ALPS index was calculated in the hemisphere ipsilateral to the occlusion (ipsilesional ALPS). Favorable outcome at 90 days was defined as modified Rankin Scale (mRS) 0-2. Multivariable logistic regression identified independent predictors, with covariates (admission National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale [NIHSS] score, LDL cholesterol, and smoking status) prespecified on clinical grounds rather than selected by univariate screening. Incremental discriminative value was assessed by comparing nested models using receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis and the likelihood-ratio test (LRT), which is preferable to DeLong's test for nested models. Calibration (Hosmer-Lemeshow test, Nagelkerke R 2 ) and internal validation with 1,000 bootstrap resamples (optimism-corrected AUC) were performed. Interpretation Lower admission NIHSS score [adjusted odds ratio (aOR) per 1-point increase: 0.890, 95% CI: 0.813-0.976; p = 0.013] and lower LDL cholesterol (aOR per 1 mmol/L: 0.660, 95% CI: 0.472-0.923; p = 0.015) were independently associated with favorable outcome, whereas the ipsilesional ALPS index showed a directionally consistent, non-significant association (aOR per 0.1-unit increase: 1.525, 95% CI: 0.948-2.454; p = 0.082). Adding the ALPS index to a base model containing NIHSS and LDL yielded a modest but significant improvement in discrimination (AUC 0.681 to 0.699; ΔAUC = 0.018; LRT p = 0.042); calibration was adequate (Hosmer-Lemeshow p = 0.31 and 0.28), and the gain persisted after bootstrap optimism correction (ΔAUC = 0.013). Conclusion In this exploratory cohort, the ipsilesional ALPS index showed a consistent directional association with 90-day functional outcome and provided a modest but significant incremental improvement in discrimination beyond NIHSS and LDL cholesterol; the magnitude of this gain is small and requires external validation.

title: The role of vascular pathology in SMA: implications for pathogenesis and treatment.
abstract: Spinal muscular atrophy (SMA) has become a paradigm for precision medicine following the development of transformative therapies targeting the disease-causing deficiency of survival motor neuron (SMN) protein. As more than 98% of SMA cases arise from mutations in the SMN1 gene, restoration of SMN expression through nusinersen (Spinraza; Biogen, Cambridge, MA), risdiplam (Evrysdi; Roche, Basel, Switzerland) and onasemnogene abeparvovec (Zolgensma and Itvisma; AveXis, Novartis, Chicago, IL) has produced unprecedented clinical benefits and established SMA as the first treatable motor neuron disease. To date, therapeutic success has focused on rescuing motor neurons, the principal site of clinical pathology. However, growing evidence indicates that SMA is a multisystem disorder in which pathological changes extend beyond the motor unit. In particular, vascular pathology has emerged as a recurring feature across numerous affected tissues. Vascular abnormalities have been identified throughout the neuromuscular system, including the spinal cord and skeletal muscle, as well as in systemic organs such as the heart, kidney, gastrointestinal tract and spleen. Experimental studies suggest that endothelial dysfunction is a direct consequence of SMN deficiency, impairing angiogenesis, vascular maturation and vessel stability, while patient-derived biomarkers, including retinal vascular imaging and elevated circulating endothelial cells (CEC), provide evidence of ongoing endothelial dysfunction in patients. These vascular abnormalities have the potential to compromise tissue perfusion, promote local hypoxia, disrupt barrier integrity and enhance inflammatory signaling, thereby exacerbating disease progression. Collectively, the evidence suggests that SMN-dependent vascular pathology may represent an under-recognized feature of SMA pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target. Here, we review the current evidence for vascular pathology in SMA, discuss its implications for disease progression, long-term patient outcomes and therapeutic response, and consider whether vascular abnormalities are adequately addressed by existing SMN-restorative therapies.

Experimental studies suggest that endothelial dysfunction is a direct consequence of SMN deficiency, impairing angiogenesis, vascular maturation and vessel stability, while patient-derived biomarkers, including retinal vascular imaging and elevated circulating endothelial cells (CEC), provide evidence of ongoing endothelial dysfunction in patients. These vascular abnormalities have the potential to compromise tissue perfusion, promote local hypoxia, disrupt barrier integrity and enhance inflammatory signaling, thereby exacerbating disease progression. Collectively, the evidence suggests that SMN-dependent vascular pathology may represent an under-recognized feature of SMA pathogenesis and a potential therapeutic target. Here, we review the current evidence for vascular pathology in SMA, discuss its implications for disease progression, long-term patient outcomes and therapeutic response, and consider whether vascular abnormalities are adequately addressed by existing SMN-restorative therapies.

title: MEMOIR-VLM-a multimodal vision-language model for Alzheimer's disease classification and question answering.
abstract: Introduction Alzheimer's disease (AD) affects an estimated 55 million people worldwide and is projected to nearly double by 2050, creating a need for scalable, non-invasive AI systems that can classify disease stage, support multimodal clinical reasoning, and interact in natural language. Most deep learning work on AD focuses on single-modality classification without natural-language interaction and typically assumes complete input data. Methods We present MEMOIR-VLM (Multimodal Encoder with Missing-modality and Open-ended Inference for Retrieval), a modular two-stage vision-language framework trained and evaluated on 2,363 ADNI subjects. The first stage is a missing-modality-aware encoder that fuses T1-weighted MRI and DTI fractional anisotropy maps with structured clinical scores via cross-attention fusion with stochastic modality dropout, allowing a single set of weights to operate on any of the seven non-empty modality subsets without imputation. After CLIP/InfoNCE contrastive pretraining, the encoder is fine-tuned for multi-task prediction of 3-way diagnosis, binary diagnosis, CDR-SB, age, and sex. The second stage extends the frozen encoder into a retrieval-augmented generation pipeline for case-based reasoning and open-ended visual question answering. Results On held-out ADNI test data, with CDR-SB excluded from the inputs to remove a cognitive-score leak, the encoder achieved 91.3% balanced accuracy for CN vs. dementia and 68.2% balanced accuracy for 3-class diagnosis (macro-F1 = 0.681); age was predicted with a 5.96-year MAE. When the diagnosis field was withheld from retrieved captions, no evaluated LLM exceeded a retrieval-only k-NN majority vote (0.673), which itself closely matched the encoder's 3-class accuracy (0.682). The RAG-VQA layer showed strong text fidelity (BERTScore = 0.894; SBERT cosine similarity = 0.811). Zero-shot external validation on OASIS-3 (1,048 subjects, no diffusion data) retained 78.7% balanced accuracy for CN vs. impaired (AUC = 0.889) using identical ADNI-trained weights with the DTI branch masked. Discussion MEMOIR-VLM combines missing-modality-aware multimodal encoding, multi-task clinical prediction, and retrieval-grounded natural-language reasoning within a single modular framework. The results support using the encoder, optionally with k-NN voting, as the diagnostic component and the RAG-VQA layer as an interpretable natural-language interface that surfaces comparable cases and readable clinical summaries. The external validation results further demonstrate the practical value of the missing-modality mechanism when an imaging modality is unavailable.

title: A systematic review of machine learning approaches for MRI-based brain tumor analysis.
abstract: Machine learning is now widely applied to magnetic resonance imaging-based brain tumor analysis, with task-specific performance metrics: the Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) quantifies segmentation overlap, while the area under the curve (AUC) and accuracy measure classification performance. A PRISMA 2020 systematic review was conducted, searching Scopus, Web of Science, PubMed, and IEEE Xplore, and identified 213 eligible studies published between January 2018 and the final search date of March 16, 2026. Segmentation performance was synthesized by random-effects meta-analysis and classification performance was summarized descriptively. Classification, detection, and grading tasks dominated the literature, followed by segmentation; U-Net variants were the most frequent architectures, with transformer-based models growing fastest. The pooled mean DSC was 0.871 (95% CI: 0.852-0.889) with a 95% prediction interval of 0.7880.953, and heterogeneity was extreme ( I 2 = 99.9%), so the pooled mean should be read as a descriptive summary of the literature rather than a single underlying effect. The descriptive mean AUC across classification studies was 0.960. Methodological gaps were pervasive: only 18.8% of studies incorporated explainability, only 18.8% performed external validation, and none reported robustness metrics. Benchmark accuracy has outpaced clinical evidence: until models are validated on independent cohorts, evaluated for robustness under realistic acquisition shifts, and made interpretable to clinicians, reported performance is unlikely to translate into patient care.

title: Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging in the diagnosis and assessment of Parkinson's disease.
abstract: Parkinson's disease (PD) is a progressive neurodegenerative disorder characterized primarily by the progressive loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta (SNpc); noradrenergic neurons in the locus coeruleus (LC) are also frequently affected. Because clinical motor symptoms usually emerge only after substantial neurodegeneration has occurred, there is a compelling need for noninvasive imaging biomarkers capable of detecting early pathological changes. Neuromelanin-sensitive magnetic resonance imaging (NM-MRI) generates neuromelanin-related image contrast in the SNpc and LC and can indirectly reflect the structural integrity of these catecholaminergic nuclei. Current evidence suggests that NM-MRI may be useful for distinguishing patients with PD from healthy controls, supporting the differential diagnosis of selected atypical parkinsonian syndromes and essential tremor, assessing disease stage, monitoring longitudinal change, and evaluating high-risk individuals in the prodromal phase. This review provides an updated account of recent advances in the use of NM-MRI for diagnostic support, differential diagnosis, prodromal assessment, longitudinal monitoring, multimodal imaging, and artificial intelligence-based analysis, and discusses its clinical role relative to other imaging and fluid biomarkers. Combining NM-MRI with complementary imaging measures, such as quantitative susceptibility mapping and diffusion MRI, and with automated analytical methods may further enhance pathological characterization and quantitative assessment. However, the available evidence is derived largely from single-center or case-control studies with limited sample sizes. Substantial variability may arise from differences in scanners, magnetic field strengths, acquisition protocols, and analytical methods, while independent external validation and prospective multicenter longitudinal evidence remain limited. The biological basis of the NM-MRI signal has not been fully established, and artificial intelligence models developed for NM-MRI remain vulnerable to overfitting, limited interpretability, and limited cross-center generalizability. Accordingly, NM-MRI cannot currently serve as a stand-alone diagnostic tool for PD or replace diagnosis based on comprehensive clinical assessment. It is better regarded as a promising complementary imaging biomarker and research tool. Before NM-MRI can be widely used for routine clinical diagnosis, disease monitoring, or as a clinical trial outcome measure, acquisition and analytical methods must be further standardized, and its performance must be evaluated in large, prospective, multicenter longitudinal studies.

title: Altered hippocampal morphology and its association with gait impairment in idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus.
abstract: Background and purpose: This study aimed to characterize structural alterations of the hippocampus associated with idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus (INPH), and to explore their relationship with gait disturbances in affected patients. Methods A total of 48 patients with INPH and 25 β-amyloid-negative healthy controls underwent MRI-based, vertex-wise three-dimensional hippocampal shape analysis. Additionally, all participants received 18F-florbetaben positron emission tomography to assess amyloid status. Results Hippocampal shape analysis revealed marked bilateral deformation in the INPH group compared to controls. Both hippocampi exhibited elongation and narrowing, with the middle and posterior regions showing upward curvature, indicating vertical displacement from the hippocampal body to the tail. The normalized hippocampal volume was significantly smaller in INPH patients. No substantial volumetric or morphological differences were observed between amyloid-positive and amyloid-negative individuals within the INPH group. Notably, localized shape deformities correlated with performance on the Timed Up and Go and 10-meter walk tests, more prominently in the right hippocampus. Bilateral inward deformations at the superomedial tail and inferior body of the hippocampus were consistently linked to worse gait performance. Furthermore, smaller right normalized hippocampal volumes were negatively associated with gait test outcomes. Conclusion These findings indicate that INPH is associated with characteristic hippocampal shape abnormalities. The observed associations between hippocampal morphology and gait disturbances suggest that the hippocampus may contribute to gait and postural control in INPH.

title: Is admission lactate an independent prognostic marker or a reflection of injury severity in severe traumatic brain injury?
abstract: Objective Although admission lactate is associated with poor outcomes after severe traumatic brain injury, its independent prognostic value remains uncertain. This study aimed to determine whether admission lactate is an independent prognostic marker or primarily a reflection of injury severity. Methods In a two-center retrospective study of patients with sTBI (GCS ≤ 8) (development cohort, n = 287; external validation cohort, n = 185), we assessed whether the association between admission lactate and 30-day mortality remained independent of established severity markers (age, GCS, pupillary reactivity, and Rotterdam CT score) and quantified the incremental prognostic value of lactate beyond this severity baseline, with external validation. Exploratory in vitro experiments in hypoxic SH-SY5Y cells were performed as a secondary analysis to examine cellular responses to lactate under hypoxic conditions. Results Thirty-day mortality was 42.2% in the development cohort and 36.8% in the external validation cohort. Admission lactate was significantly associated with mortality on univariable analysis (OR per mmol/L, 1.50; 95% CI, 1.30-1.73). After adjustment for severity markers, the adjusted OR was 1.19 per mmol/L (95% CI, 1.00-1.42; P = 0.051), indicating a positive association with limited precision. Consistent with this finding, lactate provided minimal incremental prognostic value beyond the severity baseline (ΔAUC, +0.005; P = 0.31), and these results were reproduced in the external validation cohort. Nevertheless, in vitro experiments suggested a potential biological activity of lactate that warrants further investigation. Conclusion In these two selected adult sTBI cohorts, admission lactate was associated with 30-day mortality but provided little incremental prognostic information beyond established neurological severity markers. Its role should therefore be interpreted as adjunctive rather than as a stand-alone prognostic factor. The exploratory in vitro findings warrant further mechanistic investigation.

title: SCMamba-SAM: transferring knowledge from natural images to medical tasks.
abstract: Background and objective The Segment Anything Model (SAM) has drawn significant attention because of its powerful performance in generating high-quality objectmasks. Despite its superior performance in handling natural images, SAM exhibits significant performance degradation when applied to medical images due to the substantial domain gap between natural and medical images. In addition, the specific characteristics of medical images, such as strong heterogeneity, low contrast, and wide individual variation, further raise dificulties in segmenting medical images. Methods To bridge the semantic gap between natural and medical images, we propose an adaption framework, named SCMamba-SAM. It employs a foundational image encoder constructed by integrating the pre-trained encoder of SAM and Low-Rank Adaption technique. The Encoding Mamba Adapter adopts the spatial- and channel-Mamba blocks to capture task-related global features. Additionally, an enhanced mask decoder with deep supervision has been developed to eliminate the requirement for a prompt encoder, thereby transforming SAM into a fully automated and highly accurate image segmentation model. Results Extensive experiments were performed on six public lesion segmentation datasets in different imaging modalities and body parts. The proposed SCMamba-SAM not only achieved performance superior to that of SOTA methods, quantitatively and qualitatively, but also exhibited high generalization. Conclusion SCMamba-SAM holds promise as a useful tool for clinicians to diagnose and quantify lesions, providing important information for treatment decisions and surgery planning.

title: Advances in artificial intelligence-driven MRI research in Alzheimer's disease.
abstract: Alzheimer's disease (AD), the most prevalent neurodegenerative disorder, poses substantial challenges for early diagnosis and longitudinal monitoring-two cornerstones of effective clinical management and therapeutic intervention. Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI), owing to its non-invasiveness and high spatial resolution, has emerged as an indispensable tool in AD research. In recent years, artificial intelligence (AI), particularly deep learning (DL) and machine learning (ML) techniques, has demonstrated remarkable potential for automating MRI analysis, extracting subtle imaging features, and supporting objective disease prediction. This review comprehensively summarizes the latest advances in AI-driven MRI applications for AD diagnosis, staging, prognosis, and adjuvant therapeutic monitoring. It highlights key progress in AI model development, multimodal data processing, and clinical translational value. Furthermore, current bottlenecks, including data heterogeneity, model interpretability, and real-world deployment, are systematically discussed, and future directions are outlined to enhance the precision and clinical utility of AI-assisted MRI in AD. Overall, AI-MRI has evolved from laboratory validation toward early clinical adoption, with explainability and multi-center generalizability identified as critical priorities in the next research phase.

title: PFOCUS study protocol: a prospective case-control study investigating genetic, haemodynamic, and platelet function in migraine with aura with or without patent foramen ovale.
abstract: Background Migraine with aura (MA) is associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke, particularly in young individuals without conventional vascular risk factors. A growing body of evidence indicates a strong association between MA and patent foramen ovale (PFO), the prevalence of which is up to three times higher in patients with MA than in the general population. The mechanisms underlying this association remain incompletely understood and are likely to extend beyond paradoxical embolism. Methods and design PFOCUS is a prospective, monocentric, observational case-control study designed to investigate the genetic, neurosonological, and hematological determinants linking MA and PFO. Specifically, the study evaluates whether genetic variants, particularly within the Notch signaling pathway, contribute to the coexistence of PFO and MA, and whether these patients display distinct cerebrovascular and prothrombotic profiles. As exploratory aims, the study will assess whether aura phenotypes and the distribution of MRI lesions are associated with different haemodynamic and prothrombotic profiles, potentially identifying clinically relevant subgroups within MA.A total of 240 patients with MA will be enrolled and classified as right-to-left shunt (RLS)-positive or RLS-negative on the basis of contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler (TCD), used as a surrogate marker of PFO. Participants will undergo comprehensive phenotyping including genetic testing by whole-exome sequencing, neurosonological assessment of right-to-left shunt, cerebral microemboli detection, dynamic cerebral autoregulation and cerebral vasomotor reactivity (VMR), and platelet function testing. The primary endpoint is the difference in the frequency of NOTCH3 gene variants between groups. Secondary endpoints include associations with other panel genes, correlation with shunt size, and differences in haemodynamic and platelet function parameters. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07349004. Discussion PFOCUS aims to identify a biologically distinct phenotype of MA associated with PFO, potentially driven by genetic predisposition and vascular dysfunction. Its findings may inform stroke risk stratification and open new avenues for personalized preventive strategies in patients with MA. Clinical trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier NCT07349004 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07349004).
originalAbstract:
Background

Migraine with aura (MA) is associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke, particularly in young individuals without conventional vascular risk factors. A growing body of evidence indicates a strong association between MA and patent foramen ovale (PFO), the prevalence of which is up to three times higher in patients with MA than in the general population. The mechanisms underlying this association remain incompletely understood and are likely to extend beyond paradoxical embolism.

Methods and design

PFOCUS is a prospective, monocentric, observational case-control study designed to investigate the genetic, neurosonological, and hematological determinants linking MA and PFO. Specifically, the study evaluates whether genetic variants, particularly within the Notch signaling pathway, contribute to the coexistence of PFO and MA, and whether these patients display distinct cerebrovascular and prothrombotic profiles. As exploratory aims, the study will assess whether aura phenotypes and the distribution of MRI lesions are associated with different haemodynamic and prothrombotic profiles, potentially identifying clinically relevant subgroups within MA.A total of 240 patients with MA will be enrolled and classified as right-to-left shunt (RLS)-positive or RLS-negative on the basis of contrast-enhanced transcranial Doppler (TCD), used as a surrogate marker of PFO. Participants will undergo comprehensive phenotyping including genetic testing by whole-exome sequencing, neurosonological assessment of right-to-left shunt, cerebral microemboli detection, dynamic cerebral autoregulation and cerebral vasomotor reactivity (VMR), and platelet function testing. The primary endpoint is the difference in the frequency of NOTCH3 gene variants between groups. Secondary endpoints include associations with other panel genes, correlation with shunt size, and differences in haemodynamic and platelet function parameters. ClinicalTrials.gov: NCT07349004.

Discussion

PFOCUS aims to identify a biologically distinct phenotype of MA associated with PFO, potentially driven by genetic predisposition and vascular dysfunction. Its findings may inform stroke risk stratification and open new avenues for personalized preventive strategies in patients with MA.

Clinical trial registration

ClinicalTrials.gov, identifier NCT07349004 (https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT07349004).

title: Normative functional network localization of gray matter alterations in idiopathic generalized epilepsy.
abstract: Objective Idiopathic generalized epilepsy (IGE) has traditionally been considered a non-lesional epilepsy syndrome on conventional MRI, yet voxel-based morphometry (VBM) studies have reported subtle gray matter (GM) abnormalities across diverse brain regions. These findings remain spatially heterogeneous and difficult to reconcile. We aimed to characterize the normative functional connectivity patterns associated with reported GM alterations in IGE using functional connectivity network mapping (FCNM), and to explore whether these spatially heterogeneous findings show a reproducible pattern of observed network overlap. Methods We systematically identified 18 whole-brain VBM studies of IGE, including 111 reported peak coordinates from 1,492 participants. Coordinates reflecting both increased and decreased GM were pooled in the primary analysis to characterize normative connectivity patterns associated with reported GM alterations irrespective of alteration direction. Using resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI) data from a normative discovery cohort (Human Connectome Project, N = 1,093), we mapped the functional connectivity of these GM coordinates to identify a convergent IGE-related network. The reproducibility of the observed spatial pattern was explored using an independent, cross-scanner validation cohort (Southwest University Adult Lifespan Dataset, N = 329) and two alternative seed sizes (1-mm and 7-mm radii). Results Reported GM alterations in IGE were associated with an observed distributed normative functional connectivity pattern involving the bilateral middle temporal gyri, bilateral thalami, left superior frontal gyrus, and right putamen. In the HCP discovery analysis, this network showed the greatest observed overlap with the subcortical network (overlap proportion = 42.77%) and secondary correspondence with the default mode network (DMN; overlap proportion = 11.06%). Analysis using the independent SALD connectome showed a similar descriptive pattern, with the greatest observed overlap again involving the subcortical network (overlap proportion = 43.98%), whereas DMN correspondence was weaker. Conclusion Reported GM alterations in IGE converge most robustly onto a subcortical normative functional network involving the thalamus and putamen, with additional DMN involvement observed primarily in the HCP discovery analysis. These findings provide preliminary, descriptive evidence that reported GM alterations in IGE are associated with a reproducible subcortical normative connectivity pattern across two connectome datasets, although the available analyses do not establish above-chance or disease-specific network convergence.

title: Admission TRIAGES score for unfavorable functional outcome after traumatic brain injury: association, prognostic performance, and comparison with the Glasgow coma scale.
abstract: Background The Trauma Rating Index in Age, Glasgow Coma Scale, Respiratory rate, and Systolic blood pressure (TRIAGES) is a simple trauma score that has shown prognostic value for short-term mortality in traumatic brain injury (TBI), but its relationship with functional outcome remains insufficiently characterized. Methods We conducted a retrospective single-center cohort study of adults with TBI admitted between June 2017 and May 2026. The primary exposure was the TRIAGES score calculated using age and the first GCS, respiratory rate, and systolic blood pressure values recorded at initial emergency department presentation before any in-hospital therapeutic intervention. Admission GCS was defined as the GCS value obtained at this same initial assessment. The primary outcome was unfavorable functional status at hospital discharge, defined as a discharge Glasgow Outcome Scale (GOS) score of 1-3. Multivariable logistic regression, restricted cubic spline analysis, receiver operating characteristic (ROC) analysis, calibration, Brier score, decision curve analysis, bootstrap internal validation, sensitivity analyses, and subgroup analyses were performed. Results Among 753 patients, 181 (24.0%) had an unfavorable functional outcome. Each 1-point increase in TRIAGES was independently associated with higher odds of unfavorable functional status after adjustment for sex, injury mechanism, number of non-reactive pupils, and Rotterdam CT score (adjusted odds ratio 2.81, 95% confidence interval 2.29-3.45; p < 0.001). The association was approximately linear (P for non-linearity = 0.366). TRIAGES alone achieved an area under the ROC curve (AUC) of 0.905 compared with 0.890 for admission GCS alone (ΔAUC = 0.015, 95% CI 0.001-0.029; paired DeLong p = 0.034). Within this cohort, a Youden index-derived threshold of TRIAGES ≥3 yielded a sensitivity of 0.956 and specificity of 0.701. Bootstrap internal validation showed an optimism-corrected AUC of 0.905, and the findings remained consistent across multiple sensitivity analyses. Conclusion Higher TRIAGES scores at initial emergency presentation were independently associated with unfavorable functional status at hospital discharge in adults with TBI. TRIAGES showed good prognostic performance and a small within-cohort increase in discrimination relative to admission GCS alone while retaining the practical advantage of using only four routinely available variables. Prospective multicenter studies with external validation and standardized long-term functional outcomes are warranted.

title: Revisiting the MS paradox: automated 2.5D FLAIR segmentation and DTI microstructural profiling reveals dissociation between lesion burden and reference-like intralesional tract profiles.
abstract: Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) reveals macroscopic lesion burden in multiple sclerosis (MS) but correlates poorly with clinical phenotype, a phenomenon known as the clinico-radiological paradox. While diffusion tensor imaging (DTI) metrics assess microstructural damage, standard whole-lesion averaging may obscure microstructurally spared white matter within heterogeneous plaques. We propose a fully automated, multimodal pipeline to identify and quantify reference-like intralesional segments (RLIS) within MS lesions (i.e., the cluster exhibiting maximum feature-space similarity to subject-specific, lesion-spared reference tissue). A modified 2.5D U-Net, developed and evaluated on a cohort of 75 MS patients (115 series), performed automated FLAIR lesion segmentation. In an independent cohort of 100 MS subjects, intralesional DTI metrics (FA and MD) were extracted along streamlines reconstructed via Constrained Spherical Deconvolution tractography. Unsupervised clustering algorithms, validated against a subject-specific, lesion-spared reference CST streamlines (internal capsule), identified operationally defined reference-like segments. The 2.5D U-Net achieved robust segmentation performance (DSC: 0.732, VC: 0.954), exhibited higher nominal metrics in a contextual benchmark comparison (DSC: 0.682, VC: 0.864). Across the clinical cohort, lesion count (11-131) and volume (0.54-57.3 mL) varied widely. Among the evaluated clustering methods, K-Means and Gaussian Mixture Models proved to be the most conservative, identifying median reference-like segment proportions of 26% and 22%, respectively. Crucially, the proportion of reference-like intralesional segments showed no significant monotonic association with macroscopic lesion volume or count. This automated framework successfully integrates robust deep learning-based lesion segmentation with tract-specific analysis to quantify the proportion of reference-like intralesional segments. The observed dissociation between overall lesion burden and RLIS suggests that this index serves as a promising candidate metric for exploring microstructural features that may contribute to the clinico-radiological paradox.

title: Advances in artificial intelligence for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis of neurological diseases: a systematic literature review.
abstract: Background Brain imaging is central to the structural, functional, metabolic, and neurophysiological characterization of neurological disease, yet interpretation remains constrained by heterogeneity in acquisition, annotation, expertise, and clinical context. Objective This systematic literature review evaluates recent artificial intelligence approaches for brain imaging and computer-aided diagnosis, with emphasis on methods, modalities, neurological diseases, diagnostic tasks, datasets, validation practices, and translational limitations. Methods The review followed PRISMA 2020 and covered peer-reviewed English-language studies published from January 2020 through June 2026. Eight information sources were searched using database-specific terms for artificial intelligence, neuroimaging, neurological disease, and diagnostic analysis. The search identified 1,078 records; 236 duplicates were removed, 842 unique records were screened, 258 full texts were assessed, and 123 studies were included after a record-level eligibility re-audit. Heterogeneous evidence was synthesized narratively and by descriptive mapping rather than meta-analysis. Results MRI was frequently represented in the included studies and auxiliary mapping data; CT was commonly used in acute stroke and intracranial hemorrhage; PET supported selected molecular and differential-diagnosis studies; fMRI and diffusion imaging were used for network and white-matter analysis; and EEG extended the scope to neurophysiological diagnosis. CNN and three-dimensional networks were commonly reported, while attention, Transformer, graph, self-supervised, generative, multimodal, and foundation-model approaches appeared in selected recent studies. Stroke, dementia, and brain tumors were frequently represented, but heterogeneous populations, outcomes, and incomplete validation extraction precluded ranking diseases, modalities, architectures, or validation strategies. Conclusion The evidence suggests movement from task-specific pattern recognition toward multimodal and context-rich decision support in selected settings, but it does not establish uniform methodological superiority or clinical maturity. Dependable translation requires patient-level data governance, transparent reporting, uncertainty estimation, independent multicenter testing, prospective workflow evaluation, and clinically meaningful endpoints.

title: Deep brain stimulation and spinal cord stimulation for chronic disorders of consciousness: a decade of clinical evidence, mechanistic insights, and critical appraisal.
abstract: Deep brain stimulation (DBS) and spinal cord stimulation (SCS) have been investigated for over four decades as neuromodulatory treatments for chronic disorders of consciousness (DOC), including the vegetative state/unresponsive wakefulness syndrome (VS/UWS) and the minimally conscious state (MCS), for which no disease-modifying pharmacological therapy exists. This narrative review synthesizes literature published between 2016 and 2026 on the neurobiological rationale, clinical evidence, neurophysiological biomarkers, and safety of DBS and SCS for chronic DOC. The 'mesocircuit hypothesis', supported by human intraoperative electrophysiology and nonhuman primate causal manipulation, provides a coherent rationale for central thalamic and centromedian-parafascicular targeting. Across case series, cohort studies, and individual patient data meta-analyses, both DBS and SCS produce clinically meaningful improvement in a minority of patients, consistently more often in MCS (63-74% response) than in VS/UWS (26-30% response), with younger age and shorter injury-to-treatment interval predicting better outcomes. However, the two largest individual patient data meta-analyses of DBS concur that current evidence is insufficient to conclude that stimulation alters the natural history of neurological recovery beyond what would be expected from patient selection and spontaneous recovery, and adverse event rates (8.1% for SCS, 18.2% for DBS) indicate non-trivial surgical risk in this vulnerable population. Neurophysiological and neuroimaging biomarkers derived from EEG, functional near-infrared spectroscopy, functional MRI, and FDG-PET show promise for objective outcome prediction but await prospective validation. We conclude that DBS and SCS remain experimental, mechanistically motivated but not yet definitively proven therapies for chronic DOC, and that adequately powered randomized controlled trials, biomarker-guided patient selection, and dedicated ethical frameworks are needed before either modality can be recommended outside of research settings.

title: Transformers for fMRI analysis: from spatiotemporal modeling to brain foundation models.
abstract: Functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) serves as a pivotal tool for investigating the functional organization and dynamic connectivity of the human brain, indirectly reflecting neural activity through blood oxygen level-dependent (BOLD) signals. However, the high-dimensional spatiotemporal structure, prominent noise interference, and inter-individual variability of fMRI data pose significant challenges for traditional modeling methods in characterizing complex brain functional patterns. In recent years, the Transformer architecture has gained significant traction in fMRI data analysis, leveraging its self-attention mechanism to model global dependencies. It has demonstrated superior performance in tasks such as brain disease classification, functional connectivity modeling, and brain representation learning. Compared to convolutional and recurrent neural networks, Transformers can more effectively capture long-range spatiotemporal dependencies and offer stronger structural scalability and cross-task transfer potential. To systematically map the development of this field, this paper proposes a unified taxonomy for Transformer-fMRI methods based on modeling dimensions. It categorizes existing research into four primary paradigms: temporal modeling, spatial modeling, spatiotemporal joint modeling, and self-supervised learning, providing a comparative analysis of their structural characteristics and applicable scenarios. Furthermore, this paper summarizes the key challenges regarding computational complexity, data dependency, and interpretability, while exploring the integration of neuroscientific priors with large-scale pre-trained models. Finally, we discuss future directions for Transformers in the construction of brain foundation models and their clinical utility.

title: Cortical surface morphometry changes following combined translingual neural stimulation with the portable neuromodulation stimulator and physical therapy in patients with mild-to-moderate traumatic brain injury: a pilot study.
abstract: Background Traumatic brain injury (TBI) often causes persistent balance and gait deficits, especially in mild-to-moderate TBI (mmTBI). Physical therapy is standard but often limited as a standalone treatment. Translingual neural stimulation (TLNS) is an emerging neuromodulation approach combining cranial nerve stimulation with targeted exercise to promote neuroplasticity and recovery. Its effects on cortical surface morphometry in mmTBI remain uninvestigated. Methods This secondary analysis used data from a completed clinical trial (NCT02158494). Nine chronic mmTBI patients underwent a two-week intervention combining TLNS (PoNS®) with targeted exercise training; no untreated, physical-therapy-only, or sham group was included. Balance and gait were assessed via the Sensory Organization Test (SOT) and Dynamic Gait Index (DGI) before and after the two-week in-lab phase. High-resolution T1-weighted MRI was acquired at both time points. Cortical thickness (CT), fractal dimensionality (FD), gyrification index (GI), and sulcal depth (SD) were analyzed using CAT12 with non-parametric permutation testing and TFCE correction. Results SOT and DGI scores improved significantly; due to the single-group design, these pre-post changes cannot be attributed to TLNS, physical therapy, or their combination. Widespread pre-post CT increases occurred in bilateral frontal, temporal, parietal, and cingulate regions. FD showed increases (precuneus, insula, and superior frontal gyrus) and decreases (lateral occipital, inferior temporal gyri). GI decreased in the left lingual gyrus; SD showed bidirectional changes. Exploratory correlations linked greater behavioral gains with smaller CT increases in right inferior temporal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule, and smaller FD increases in left precuneus; these were underpowered ( N = 9), uncorrected, and hypothesis-generating only. Morphometric changes in either direction cannot be assumed to reflect beneficial neuroplasticity. Conclusion In this exploratory, single-group pilot study, cortical surface morphometric changes accompanied balance and gait improvements after combined TLNS plus physical therapy in mm TBI. Without a control group, causality cannot be determined. Findings are preliminary and support randomized, sham-controlled trials, ideally with a physical-therapy-only arm.

Exploratory correlations linked greater behavioral gains with smaller CT increases in right inferior temporal gyrus and right superior parietal lobule, and smaller FD increases in left precuneus; these were underpowered (N = 9), uncorrected, and hypothesis-generating only. Morphometric changes in either direction cannot be assumed to reflect beneficial neuroplasticity.

Conclusion

In this exploratory, single-group pilot study, cortical surface morphometric changes accompanied balance and gait improvements after combined TLNS plus physical therapy in mm TBI. Without a control group, causality cannot be determined. Findings are preliminary and support randomized, sham-controlled trials, ideally with a physical-therapy-only arm.

title: UAC-Net: a unified multi-task network with aggregated contextual attention and cross-layer fusion for brain tumor segmentation and classification.
abstract: Accurate segmentation and classification of brain tumors from magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) are critical for clinical diagnosis and treatment planning. However, existing methods typically treat these two tasks independently, failing to exploit their inherent complementarity, and often struggle to capture multi-scale contextual information essential for identifying small or irregular lesions. To address these limitations, this paper proposes UAC-Net, a unified multi-task learning framework built upon a U-Net backbone that jointly optimizes tumor segmentation and classification through a shared encoder. Two core modules are introduced: (1) the Aggregated Contextual Attention (ACA) module, which enhances dynamic perception of critical lesion regions by combining local sliding-window attention with global downsampling attention across all encoder levels; and (2) the Adjacent Layer Multi-scale Feature Fusion (ALMFF) module, which enables cross-level feature interaction to enrich multi-scale representations. In the segmentation branch, ALMFF-fused features are progressively upsampled to achieve precise lesion localization; in the classification branch, ACA-enhanced deep features are aggregated via global average pooling to yield robust semantic representations for tumor typing. Experiments on two publicly available brain tumor MRI datasets demonstrate that UAC-Net achieves competitive and consistent performance compared with several representative methods. Specifically, UAC-Net obtains a classification accuracy of 98.53% and a Dice coefficient of 81.39% on the Figshare dataset, and achieves 99.07% classification accuracy and 86.61% Dice coefficient on the BRISC 2025 dataset. These findings suggest that integrating contextual attention and cross-layer feature fusion within a unified multi-task framework is a promising approach for joint brain tumor segmentation and classification.

title: Cascaded deep learning for synthesis of <sup>18</sup>F-FDG PET from <sup>18</sup>F-octreotide: model parameter optimization and performance evaluation.
abstract: Objective To investigate a cascaded conditional generative adversarial network (cGAN)-based method for synthesizing 18 F-FDG PET images from 18 F-octreotide, optimize model parameter configurations, and evaluate the quality of the synthesized images. Methods Imaging data from 71 tumor patients who underwent dual-tracer PET/CT examinations with 18 F-FDG and 18 F-octreotide between May 2022 and November 2025 were retrospectively collected. A cascaded deep learning architecture (first stage: 3D U-Net; second stage: self-attention 3D V-Net) was employed to evaluate the effects of image preprocessing, resampling size, and patch size on synthesis quality. Three preprocessing strategies (log transformation, normalization, and a combined approach) were compared. Image quality was assessed using five objective metrics (SSIM, PSNR, MSE, MAE, and NMI) and Likert 5-point ratings from three nuclear medicine physicians; liver and lesion-level SUV agreement were further evaluated. Results In the held-out test cohort ( n = 14), the combined preprocessing method (log transformation + normalization) significantly outperformed the individual methods (SSIM: 0.8454 ± 0.0328 vs. 0.7831 ± 0.0337 vs. 0.7438 ± 0.0362, P < 0.001). On the identical held-out test cohort ( n = 14), the Group 2 parameter configuration (resampling size: 256 × 256 × 512; patch size: 128 × 128 × 128) outperformed Group 1, with an SSIM of 0.8854 ± 0.0455 and a PSNR of 28.15 ± 3.35 dB, representing relative improvements of 19.1% and 83.5%, respectively, over Group 1 (paired-samples t-test, both P < 0.001). The mean Likert score was 4.53 ± 0.19. Quantitative analysis of liver SUVmean showed no significant difference between synthesized and real images ( P = 0.967, paired t-test). Lesion-level quantitative analysis demonstrated high agreement between synthetic and real 18 F-FDG images, with Pearson correlation coefficients of 1.0000, 0.9995, and 0.9991 for SUVmax and SUVmean ( n = 14) and SUVpeak ( n = 13), respectively (all P < 0.001), no significant differences on paired t-tests (all P > 0.05), and all Bland-Altman differences within the 95% limits of agreement. Conclusion The cascaded deep learning model enabled cross-tracer synthesis from 18 F-octreotide to 18 F-FDG PET images. In this exploratory, single-center pilot cohort, the optimized configuration demonstrated promising quantitative and visual performance, supporting image-synthesis feasibility and potential clinical utility of a single-injection, dual-parameter molecular imaging approach for neuroendocrine tumors. Prospective multicenter validation is warranted before any clinical application.

title: From task-specific AI to multimodal foundation models in PET/CT: a readiness framework for clinical translation.
abstract: Artificial intelligence in PET/CT is evolving from narrowly optimized systems toward reusable pretrained representations and multimodal models. PET/CT is a demanding test case because clinically meaningful interpretation must preserve quantitative molecular information while integrating anatomic CT, acquisition metadata, longitudinal examinations, and free-text imaging reports. This focused narrative review synthesizes literature reported from January 2021 through July 2026, spanning PET reconstruction and enhancement, attenuation correction, segmentation, outcome modeling, pretrained representations, vision-language systems, and agentic workflows. We distinguish task-specific models, reusable pretrained representations, promptable models, vision-language systems, generalist foundation-model candidates, and agentic systems according to demonstrated capabilities, while separately considering evaluation benchmarks. Task-specific deep learning has demonstrated promising technical performance in low-count imaging and whole-body tumor analysis, but most evidence remains retrospective and restricted by radiotracer, disease, scanner, institution, or endpoint. Emerging PET-native studies demonstrate label-efficient segmentation, image-text grounding, report generation, and modular tool orchestration; however, they do not yet establish broad cross-tracer generalization or prospective clinical benefit. We therefore propose MOSAIC-PET, an author-developed heuristic six-domain evaluation framework for PET/CT foundation models encompassing Molecular fidelity, Organ and anatomic grounding, Semantic faithfulness, Adaptability, Integration and clinical impact, and Continuous governance. MOSAIC-PET has not undergone Delphi consensus or formal validation and is intended to organize PET-specific evidence requirements rather than function as a validated clinical-readiness tool. The near-term translational priority is the development of modular, auditable systems in which validated quantitative tools and evidence-linked language outputs remain under specialist oversight, with progression from external testing to silent evaluation, assisted-use studies, clinical-impact assessment, and continuous lifecycle monitoring.

title: Predictive value of multimodal models combining CT body composition and clinical variables for short-term postoperative complications in colorectal cancer: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
abstract: Background Malnutrition and sarcopenic obesity are prevalent in colorectal cancer (CRC) and linked to adverse surgical outcomes. Conventional screening often overlooks this occult malnutrition. Preoperative computed tomography (CT)-based body composition analysis (BCA) provides objective biomarkers for muscle depletion and fat distribution. This systematic review evaluates multimodal machine learning (ML) models integrating BCA and clinical variables to predict CRC postoperative complications and inform precision nutrition strategies. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library (inception to April 13, 2026) for ML models predicting postoperative complications in CRC using BCA. Quality was assessed using PROBAST. Pooled area under the curve (AUC) was estimated via a random-effects model, alongside subgroup analyses. Results Eight studies ( n = 7,835) were included. The pooled AUC was 0.84 (95% CI: 0.76-0.89), indicating good discriminative performance, although substantial heterogeneity was present ( I 2 = 79.7%). Nomogram-based models showed a pooled AUC of 0.87 (95% CI: 0.78-0.92). For anastomotic leakage, the pooled AUC was 0.83 (95% CI: 0.35-0.98), although this estimate was imprecise because only two studies contributed to this subgroup. Conclusion Multimodal ML models integrating BCA biomarkers offer a robust, data-driven framework for preoperative risk stratification in CRC. Identifying high-risk body composition phenotypes may facilitate tailored prehabilitation and targeted immunonutrition strategies. Future efforts must prioritize standardized BCA and multi-center external validation. Systematic review registration CRD420261364363.

title: Novel AI-derived muscle ultrasound biomarkers linking nutritional status and prognosis in cancer patients.
abstract: Introduction Malnutrition and sarcopenia worsen prognosis in patients with cancer and require accessible diagnostic methods for assessing muscle quantity and quality. Artificial intelligence (AI)-assisted muscle ultrasound may improve the standardization and efficiency of body-composition assessment. This study evaluated the prognostic relevance of AI-assisted rectus femoris ultrasound biomarkers within a comprehensive nutritional assessment of patients with cancer. Methods This prospective longitudinal observational cohort study included 389 patients with cancer, most of whom had tumors of digestive origin. Participants underwent longitudinal and transverse rectus femoris ultrasonography. Images were analyzed using PIIXMED™ MSK, which applies U-Net based anatomical segmentation followed by deterministic image-processing procedures. The evaluated variables included subcutaneous adipose tissue thickness (SAT), rectus femoris thickness (RFT) rectus femoris cross-sectional area (RFA), pennation angle, mean echo intensity, and the percentages of low- and medium-echogenicity pixels within the segmented region of interest, reported as the Muscle Index (Mi) and Fat Index (FATi), respectively. The muscle-area index was calculated as AreaMi = RFAxMi. Results The 389 participants had a mean age of 70.6 (10.8) years, 58.9% were men, and 53.7% ( n = 206) were classified as geriatric oncology patients (≥70 years). Malnutrition was present in 75.3% of participants, confirmed sarcopenia in 18.8% and overall mortality during follow-up was 26.5%. In univariate log-rank survival analysis, reduced muscle-area index (MiArea<1.36 cm 2 ; p = 0.014) and low muscle quality (Mi < 46%; p = 0.019) were the strongest univariate predictors of significantly shorter survival. In multivariate Cox proportional Hazards regression models adjusted for age, sex, digestive tumor location, and metastatic disease, larger rectus femoris area (RFA: HR = 0.77. 95%CI: 0.62-0.95; p < 0.05) and thickness (RFT: HR = 0.43, 95% CI: 0.19-0.99; p < 0.05) remained independent protective factors against mortality. Conversely, reduced muscle index (Mi < 47%: HR = 1.60, 95%CI: 1.05-2.06; p < 0.05) and the presence of myosteatosis (HR = 2.35, 95%CI: 1.19-4.62; p = 0.01) independently predicted an increased risk of mortality. Conclusion In cancer patients, AI-assisted rectus femoris ultrasound variables effectively predict mortality. Greater muscle area and higher muscle index (Mi > 47%) indicate a favorable prognosis. Early ultrasound assessment detects structural alterations before overt deterioration, providing a crucial window for targeted nutritional interventions to preserve muscle integrity and prevent complications.

title: Genetic risk stratification reveals distinct first-order radiomic phenotypes in hepatocellular carcinoma.
abstract: Background Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) exhibits significant morphological heterogeneity that has traditionally been attributed to etiological, environmental, and biological factors. Recent evidence suggests, however, that genetic background may influence tumor characteristics and behavior in HCC. Purpose To investigate associations between established HCC genetic risk factors and first-order radiomic features. Methods We evaluated a retrospective cohort of 210 patients with HCC who underwent contrast-enhanced MRI and genetic profiling for three established HCC risk variants (PNPLA3 rs738409-G, TM6SF2 rs58542926-T, and MAU2 rs58489806-T). We screened first-order radiomic features in the full cohort and then focused the primary analysis on 77 treatment-naive patients whose tumor morphology had not been modified by therapy. Patients were stratified into at-risk (≥1 risk allele, n=52) and wild-type (no risk alleles, n=25) groups. Eighteen first-order radiomic features were screened using the Mann-Whitney U test and AUC analysis. The leading feature, kurtosis, was then subjected to univariate and multivariate analysis for clinical and imaging features to identify any confounding effect. In addition, a 10-fold cross-validated cutpoint stability, sensitivity analysis, and Cox/Kaplan-Meier survival analysis were also conducted. Results Among 18 features, kurtosis best distinguished at-risk from wild-type genotypes in treatment-naive patients (AUC = 0.67, p=0.014), with wild-type tumors showing more uniform, sharply peaked intensity patterns. Tumor volume correlated modestly with kurtosis (Spearman's ρ=0.45, p<0.0001), but volume alone did not discriminate genotype (Mann-Whitney U, p=0.3994). The genotype-kurtosis association remained significant after adjusting for volume and shape (ANCOVA, p=0.029) and strengthened after adjusting for nine clinical/demographic covariates (p=0.003), indicating kurtosis reflects biological information beyond tumor size. The empirical cutpoint was stable across 10-fold cross-validation (mean=3.35, SD = 0.05), and results were unchanged in sensitivity analysis. Kurtosis was not associated with overall survival (Cox HR = 1.19, p=0.13). No genotype-related discrimination was observed in the pooled full cohort, consistent with treatment-related alteration of tumor texture. Conclusions In a cohort of 210 genetically profiled patients with HCC, genotype-related radiomic features were not apparent when treated and untreated tumors were analyzed together. However, restricting the analysis to the treatment-naive subgroup (n=77) revealed tumor kurtosis as a reproducible, biologically plausible first-order imaging correlate of established HCC genetic risk status.

title: The clinical value of ultrasound radiomics combined with clinical data nomogram in predicting cervical lymph node metastasis of papillary thyroid carcinoma.
abstract: Objectives To evaluate the predictive value of a nomogram incorporating ultrasound and clinical features for cervical lymph node metastasis (CLNM) in patients with thyroid cancer. Methods A retrospective analysis was conducted on patients pathologically diagnosed with papillary thyroid carcinoma (PTC) between April 2024 and January 2025. Radiomics features were extracted from two-dimensional thyroid ultrasound images, and feature selection was performed using the least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO). Five classifiers were compared, and logistic regression was selected to construct the radiomics model. A clinical-radiomics model integrating the radiomics score and clinical predictors, together with a standalone clinical model, was developed using multivariable logistic regression. Model discrimination, calibration, and clinical utility were evaluated in a held-out internal validation set. Results Sex, Radscore, age, and thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) levels were identified as independent predictors of CLNM in patients with PTC. Based on these variables, radiomics, clinical, and clinical radiomics models were constructed; the models achieved area under the curve (AUC) values of 0.735, 0.792, and 0.867, respectively, in the validation set.
