title: [Development of the autotransplantation technique: from freehand surgery to a digital 3D workflow].
abstract: Autotransplantation of teeth is an effective treatment option for tooth replacement, particularly in young patients. Traditionally, the recipient socket is prepared freehand by repeatedly fitting the donor tooth, which may result in prolonged extra-alveolar time and potential damage to the periodontal ligament. With the introduction of cone beam computed tomography imaging, digital planning and 3D printing technology, it has become possible to fabricate a patient-specific replica of the donor tooth. This allows the recipient socket to be prepared accurately, thus limiting intraoperative adjustments and extra-alveolar time.

title: Multi-regional debridement and staged reconstruction for fracture-related infection after intramedullary nailing.
abstract: Late fracture-related infection (FRI) after intramedullary nailing may extend beyond the fracture site to involve the medullary canal, nail entry site, and locking screw tracts. This retrospective cohort study evaluated a staged protocol incorporating systematic multi-regional debridement of the entire nail-related infection pathway. We reviewed 47 patients treated between January 2017 and January 2025, all of whom had fracture nonunion and an interval of at least 3 months from the first documented confirmation of FRI to admission. Stage I included intramedullary nail removal; systematic multi-regional debridement of the fracture/nonunion site, nail entry site, entire medullary canal, and proximal and distal locking screw tracts; locking plate fixation; and temporary vancomycin-loaded polymethyl methacrylate cement placement for dead-space management and induced membrane formation. Definitive Stage II reconstruction included the removal of the temporary plate construct and cement, repeat debridement, bone grafting, and definitive fixation with a new internal locking plate after clinical and laboratory infection quiescence and intraoperative reassessment. The cohort included 21 tibial and 26 femoral cases, with a mean follow-up of 25.3 ± 14.1 months. Two patients had confirmed persistent infection requiring repeat debridement before definitive Stage II reconstruction. No confirmed recurrence or unplanned surgical debridement for suspected recurrence occurred after definitive reconstruction. Union after the index Stage II reconstruction was achieved in 44 of 47 patients (93.6 %). The remaining three patients achieved union after further surgery, resulting in a final union rate of 100 %. The mean times to radiographic union and full weight-bearing were 9.7 ± 2.1 and 11.3 ± 3.8 months, respectively. Median (interquartile range) WBC count, ESR, and CRP decreased from 7.2 (6.2-9.0) × 10 9 L -1 , 39.0 (12.5-65.0) mm h -1 , and 26.5 (10.3-43.2) mg L -1 to 5.9 (5.0-7.7) × 10 9 L -1 , 17.0 (8.0-29.5) mm h -1 , and 6.3 (3.7-8.9) mg L -1 , respectively. LEFS and SF-36 scores increased from 47.0 (37.0-65.5) and 417.0 (335.0-439.0) to 70.0 (61.0-75.5) and 491.0 (480.0-516.5), whereas VAS and SAS scores decreased from 4.0 (4.0-4.0) and 45.0 (42.0-50.0) to 1.0 (0.0-1.0) and 32.0 (29.5-37.0), respectively (all p≤0 .001). These findings support the feasibility of this staged protocol in selected patients with late post-intramedullary-nailing FRI and nonunion.

title: Clinical Impact of Trastuzumab Deruxtecan in Patients With HER2-Positive Advanced Gastric Cancer and Ascites: Findings From the EN-DEAVOR Study.
abstract: Purpose Patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2)-positive advanced gastric cancer (AGC) and ascites have poor prognosis and are often excluded from clinical trials. Thus, evidence on the effect of trastuzumab deruxtecan (T-DXd) in this population remains limited. Materials and methods This subgroup analysis of the EN-DEAVOR (UMIN000049032) study assessed outcomes in patients with T-DXd-treated HER2-positive AGC from Japan, stratified by computed tomography-defined ascites severity: none (ascites not detected), low (confined to the upper or lower abdomen), moderate (neither low nor high), and high (diffusely present throughout the abdomen). The outcomes included overall survival (OS), real-world progression-free survival (rwPFS), ascites response rate, and incidence of grade ≥3 adverse events (AEs). Results Among 312 patients, 173, 81, 34, and 20 had no, low, moderate, and high ascites severity, respectively. The median OS was 12.35, 6.77, 6.97, and 5.13 months, respectively, and the median rwPFS was 5.32, 3.68, 3.50, and 2.76 months, respectively, for the no, low, moderate, and high severity groups. The overall ascites response rate to ascites severity was 23.0%. The median OS and rwPFS were 11.83 (95% confidence interval [CI], 7.82-18.96) and 6.64 (95% CI, 4.17-9.56) months, respectively, in responders, and 6.28 (95% CI, 4.90-7.03) and 3.15 (95% CI, 2.17-3.94) months, respectively, in non-responders. Grade ≥3 AE incidence was comparable across subgroups. Conclusions T-DXd demonstrated efficacy and a manageable safety profile in patients with HER2-positive AGC, including those with severe ascites. The ascites response correlated with improved outcomes.

title: Comparison of Proximal Gastrectomy With Double-Tract Reconstruction and Total Gastrectomy for Stage II-III Upper Gastric Cancer: A Dual-Institutional Propensity Score-Matched Analysis.
abstract: Purpose Total gastrectomy (TG) is the standard treatment for stage II-III upper gastric cancer, whereas proximal gastrectomy is primarily used for early-stage disease. This study compared the oncologic and nutritional consequences, including anemia, vitamin B12 deficiency, and body composition changes, between proximal gastrectomy with double-tract reconstruction (PG-DTR) and TG. Materials and methods We retrospectively analyzed a prospectively maintained dual-institutional database of patients who underwent curative-intent PG-DTR or TG for stage II-III gastric cancer between 2015 and 2022. Machine learning-based propensity score matching balanced the clinicopathological variables. Perioperative outcomes, hematologic and nutritional parameters, computed tomography-based body composition, and survival were compared. Results After matching, 62 patient pairs were included. Complication rates were comparable between the groups. Five-year cumulative incidences of anemia (86.2% vs. 88.7%, P=0.507), iron replacement (48.7% vs. 58.3%, P=0.595), and vitamin B12 deficiency (8.9% vs. 22.3%, P=0.139) were similar. However, the 5-year cumulative incidence of vitamin B12 replacement was significantly lower after PG-DTR than after TG (46.4% vs. 95.4%, P<0.001). Longitudinal changes in body composition, body weight, hemoglobin level, albumin level, and prognostic nutritional index were similar between the groups. Five-year overall survival rates were 78.9% and 81.1% (P=0.801), and the 5-year recurrence-free survival rates were 73.0% and 78.2% (P=0.690) in the PG-DTR and TG groups, respectively. Conclusions PG-DTR showed no statistically significant differences in perioperative, nutritional, and oncologic outcomes compared with TG in this cohort. These findings should be interpreted cautiously because of the limited statistical power, and larger prospective studies are warranted.

title: Liposclerosing myxofibrous tumor of the proximal femur: a case report.
abstract: Liposclerosing myxofibrous tumor (LSMFT) is a rare fibro-osseous lesion with a strong predilection for the proximal femur, rarely seen in clinical practice and often diagnostically challenging. A 29-year-old woman who presented with left hip pain after a fall is reported. Multimodal imaging - plain radiographs, computed tomography, and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) - was performed, followed by intraoperative frozen section analysis and curettage. The residual cavity was filled with a synthetic bioactive-glass bone substitute, and the proximal femur was stabilised with a dynamic hip screw (DHS). Plain radiographs showed a geographic lytic lesion in the subtrochanteric femur with a thick sclerotic rim. Computed tomography confirmed well-defined medullary expansion with heterogeneous mineralisation. MRI demonstrated marked T2 hyperintensity consistent with myxoid stroma. Intraoperative frozen section showed a benign-appearing spindle-cell lesion; permanent histopathology on a 10×8×2 cm curettage specimen confirmed LSMFT, demonstrating the characteristic polymorphic combination of xanthomatous foci, mature adipocytes, fibrous stroma, and myxoid areas without malignant features. At the latest follow-up, 4 months postoperatively, the patient was pain-free (visual analogue scale 0) with a full, unrestricted hip range of motion and a Harris Hip Score of 99.8; full weight-bearing had been resumed by the second postoperative month. Follow-up radiographs demonstrated incorporation of the graft without evidence of local recurrence, and no complications were recorded. This case highlights the diagnostic challenges of LSMFT, the limitations of intraoperative frozen section in polymorphic fibro-osseous lesions, and the importance of structural fixation at the subtrochanteric level. Although the short-term outcome was excellent, lifelong surveillance is warranted given the reported risk of malignant transformation.

title: Fluoroscopy-Guided Intra-Articular Hip Corticosteroid Injections: Diagnostic and Therapeutic Utility, Technique, and Steroid Selection.
abstract: Intra-articular hip corticosteroid injection is a practical option for selected patients with hip pain, particularly osteoarthritis, and may also clarify whether symptoms arise from the hip rather than the lumbar spine or periarticular structures. This review evaluates the diagnostic and therapeutic utility of injections performed under fluoroscopy, summarizes technique, and discusses steroid selection and dosing. # Recent Findings Randomized trials and contemporary syntheses support clinically meaningful short-term improvement in pain and function after image-guided hip corticosteroid injection, although durability is variable and repeated-injection data remain limited. Fluoroscopy provides continuous visualization of osseous landmarks and contrast-confirmed intra-articular spread. Ultrasound avoids radiation and may be more convenient depending on physician comfort level and ultrasound skills. Safety discussions have emphasized transient systemic effects, uncertain associations with rapidly progressive osteoarthritis, and the timing of injection before arthroplasty. # Summary Fluoroscopy-guided injection remains a reliable, reproducible diagnostic and therapeutic tool when the pain generator is uncertain or short-term symptom control may facilitate rehabilitation, bridge care, or support shared surgical decision-making. Benefit depends on careful patient selection, technically confirmed intra-articular delivery, conservative dosing, and explicit counseling that relief is usually temporary and that structural disease is not reversed.

title: Connectome and Depression: Towards Precision Psychiatry Based on Brain Networks
abstract: In recent decades, the study of the human connectome —the comprehensive map of the brain's neural connections— has redefined our understanding of Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) as a spectrum of functional and structural alterations in specific brain networks. This review explores evidence on functional connectivity patterns in MDD, highlighting the involvement of networks such as the default mode network (DMN), frontoparietal network (FPN), salience network (SN), and reward circuits. We analyze patterns detected using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) and their potential as biomarkers to predict treatment response to interventions currently included in clinical guidelines and widely used in practice, such as psychotherapy, first-line antidepressants (SSRIs), transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS), electroconvulsive therapy (ECT), and sub-anesthetic doses of ketamine. For this purpose, we conducted an integrative narrative review of the scientific literature, selecting articles based on clinical relevance and methodological quality (GRADE), including meta-analyses, systematic reviews, and randomized controlled trials. These findings may contribute to a paradigm shift toward precision psychiatry, increasingly centered on the individual. Although methodological challenges persist that limit their clinical application, understanding the connectome and its relationship with MDD pathogenesis is a fundamental step toward truly personalized mental healthcare.

title: Whole-body MRI with DWIBS and choline PET/CT for detecting oligoprogressive castration-resistant prostate cancer recurrence.
abstract: The diagnostic options for patients with advanced prostate cancer have expanded with the development of next-generation imaging modalities. These include whole-body magnetic resonance imaging (WB-MRI) with diffusion-weighted whole-body imaging with background body signal suppression (DWIBS) and molecular positron emission tomography/computed tomography (PET/CT) using choline or prostate-specific membrane antigen radiotracers. Such modalities improve the detection of whole-body nodal and bony metastases in patients with advanced prostate cancer. A 63-year-old man with castration-resistant prostate cancer (CRPC) underwent stereotactic body radiotherapy (SBRT) targeting two pelvic nodal metastases identified by WB-MRI with DWIBS and subsequently confirmed by 11 C-choline PET/CT. This case highlights the potential role of 11 C-choline PET/CT and corresponding local treatment in the management of oligoprogressive CRPC.

title: Clinical and radiological comparisons of posterior labral tears with and without posterior glenohumeral instability.
abstract: Background We compare clinical and radiological characteristics and evaluate surgical outcomes of posterior labral tears based on the presence of glenohumeral instability. Methods Patients who were unresponsive to conservative treatment and underwent arthroscopic posterior labral repair were reviewed retrospectively. Patients were divided into two groups: those with glenohumeral instability (group 1) and those without (group 2). Demographic, radiological, physical examination, and intraoperative data were collected. Clinical outcomes were assessed at a minimum 2-year follow-up using the visual analog scale for pain, American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons, and Rowe scores. Results The study included a total of 85 patients (40 in group 1 and 45 in group 2) with a mean follow-up duration of 31.8±12.2 months. Patients in group 2 were older (31.4±1.0 years old, P<0.001), had longer symptom durations (30.1±5.6 months, P=0.002), and included fewer histories of trauma (16 patients, P=0.009). Competitive sports were more common in group 1 (9 patients, P=0.005), whereas weightlifting exercises were more common in group 2 (24 patients, P=0.047). Magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) underestimated incomplete posterior labral tears more frequently in group 2 than in group 1 (P=0.033). The incidence of arthroscopically detected tears among MRI-occult tears was higher in group 2 (10 patients) than in group 1 (2 patients, P=0.029). Statistically significant improvements in shoulder function were observed postoperatively in both groups. Conclusions Clinical and magnetic resonance findings of posterior labral tears without glenohumeral instability differ from those with instability. Surgical treatment achieved satisfactory clinical outcomes regardless of the presence of instability. Level of evidence: III.

title: Osteoporosis Screening Gaps Among Patients Undergoing Lumbar Fusion Surgery.
abstract: Background Osteoporosis is associated with elevated complication rates after lumbar fusion surgery. Despite this, osteoporosis remains both underscreened and undertreated in the United States. Currently, rates of dual-energy radiograph absorptiometry (DEXA) screening before lumbar fusion surgery are unknown, as is the proportion of patients who, after being diagnosed with osteoporosis, receive appropriate treatment. Therefore, the aim of this study was to assess osteoporosis screening and treatment rates among patients undergoing lumbar fusion surgery. Methods Patients older than 50 years undergoing lumbar fusion for lumbar stenosis with degenerative spondylolisthesis were identified using the TriNetX database. Patients receiving surgery for indications of malignancy or infection, as well as those with diagnoses of osteoporosis before the screening window, were excluded. The prevalence of DEXA scans in the 2 years before fusion was calculated for the overall cohort and for high-risk cohorts defined by Endocrinology Society guidelines. A secondary analysis assessed rates of osteoporosis treatment among patients receiving preoperative DEXA scans. Results Of 46,104 patients who underwent lumbar fusion surgery, only 4.5% of men and 15.6% of women received a preoperative DEXA scan in the 2 years before their fusion. Women were more likely to receive DEXA scans than men (OR, 3.93; 95% CI, 3.64 to 4.23; P < 0.001). Only 5.6% of high-risk men and 17.5% of high-risk women received preoperative DEXA screening. Among patients diagnosed with osteoporosis after DEXA screening, only 11.0% received anabolic therapy and 23.1% received antiresorptive therapy. Conclusion Despite most patients undergoing lumbar fusion being at risk of osteoporosis (and eligible for screening), a small minority were screened using DEXA in the 2 years before surgery. Efforts are warranted to increase the prevalence of DEXA screening so that osteoporosis is appropriately diagnosed and treated before lumbar fusion surgery.

title: The Incidence and Diagnosis of Intra-articular Extension With Spiral Distal Third Humerus Fractures.
abstract: Purpose Many orthopaedic injuries have associated fracture patterns that require specific diagnostic tests. The relationship between spiral distal humeral shaft fractures and intra-articular extension has not been previously assessed. The purpose of this study was therefore to identify whether there is an association between spiral distal humeral shaft fractures and intra-articular extension. Methods We conducted a retrospective review of patients with spiral distal third humeral shaft fractures (12A1, 12B1, and 12C1) from 2016 to 2021 at a single institution. We queried our electronic medical record using CPT codes (24500, 24505, 24515, and 24516) and ICD10 codes (S42.3 and S42.4). Inclusion criteria consisted of patients older than 17 years, spiral distal third humeral shaft fractures (12A1, 12B1, and 12C1), and patients with appropriate radiographic imaging. We recorded OTA fracture classification, presence of CT scan, and presence of intra-articular extension. Results Nine hundred seventeen patients were identified with humeral shaft fractures. Of those, 57 patients were included in the study with spiral distal third humerus fractures. One patient (1.8%) had intra-articular extension. Thirty patients had CT scans of the distal humerus; no additional cases of intra-articular extension beyond the single radiographically identified fracture were detected. Conclusion Distal third spiral humeral shaft fractures (AO/OTA 12A1, 12B1, and 12C1) rarely demonstrate intra-articular extension. In our cohort, only 1 case showed articular involvement and was apparent on initial radiographs. Therefore, routine CT imaging is not indicated for these fractures and should be reserved for patients with concerning clinical findings or radiographic features suggestive of intra-articular extension.

title: Atropine-Associated Central Anticholinergic Syndrome during Carotid Artery Stenting: A Case Report.
abstract: Acute neurobehavioral deterioration during carotid artery stenting (CAS) requires prompt evaluation for serious neurological complications. We report a patient in their 70s who developed profound hyperactive delirium approximately 15 minutes after receiving prophylactic intravenous atropine (0.25 mg) during CAS. The episode was characterized by severe agitation, bilateral mydriasis, and facial flushing without focal neurological deficits. Repeated angiography and subsequent neuroimaging showed no evidence of thromboembolism, intracranial hemorrhage, cerebral edema, or cerebral hyperperfusion. Contrast-induced encephalopathy and cerebral hyperperfusion syndrome were considered but were less consistent with the overall clinical, temporal, and radiographic findings. The patient returned to neurological and cognitive baseline approximately 16 hours after symptom onset without specific antidotal treatment. The close temporal relationship to atropine exposure and characteristic neurobehavioral and autonomic features favored atropine-associated central anticholinergic syndrome, which should be considered in the differential diagnosis of acute neurobehavioral deterioration during CAS.

title: Minimally invasive surgery via minimally invasive anesthesia Is laryngeal mask airway sufficient for supine percutaneous nephrolithotomy?
abstract: Introduction While endotracheal tube (ETT) is the traditional airway modality for percutaneous nephrolithotomy (PCNL), the adoption of supine positioning has opened the door for alternative strategies. Laryngeal mask airway (LMA) offers potential advantages, but its safety profile in supine PCNL remains understudied. This study aimed to compare urologic and anesthesia-related outcomes between LMA and ETT in patients undergoing ultrasound-guided supine PCNL. Methods In this retrospective study, 206 adult patients undergoing supine PCNL under general anesthesia between March 2023 and June 2024 were analyzed. Patients were grouped by airway modality: LMA (n=156) or ETT (n=50). Exclusion criteria included body mass index (BMI) >35 kg/m 2 , American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) score ≥4, chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), pregnancy, or incomplete data. Urologic outcomes included intraoperative complications, 30-day complications, and postoperative pain. Anesthesia-related outcomes included hemodynamic instability, post-anesthesia care unit (PACU) stay, airway placement/removal times, and anesthesia-related complications. Outcomes were compared between the groups, and multivariable regression and sensitivity analysis were used to adjust for confounders. Results Overall complications were significantly lower in the LMA group (13% vs. 28%, p=0.01), and LMA was negatively associated with them in univariable analysis (odds ratio [OR] 0.378, 95% confidence interval [CI] 0.174-0.821, p=0.01). LMA use remained independently associated with a reduced risk of overall anesthetic and urologic complications after ad-hoc adjustments for preoperative risk factors, stone characteristics, and intraoperative factors. Airway placement and removal times were shorter in the LMA group; otherwise, no significant differences were observed in anesthesia-related outcomes. No procedures were aborted or converted due to airway complications. Conclusions In our limited study, LMA seems to be a safe and effective alternative to ETT for airway management in appropriately selected patients undergoing supine PCNL. Prospective, randomized studies are needed to confirm these findings.

title: Assessment of survivin mRNA expression level and its serum level in patients with diabetic retinopathy.
abstract: Diabetic patients may suffer from diabetic retinopathy (DR) which may result in vision loss. Apoptosis is essential in vascular remodeling. Survivin inhibits endothelial cell apoptosis and enhances angiogenesis. Diabetic vasculopathy can increase survivin expression. Our aim is to measure the clinical significance of survivin mRNA expression and its serum level with DR as predictors for disease prognosis. Thirty patients with DR; thirty without DR and thirty healthy persons were included as controls (employees and attendants for checkup with normal HA1c level). Ophthalmic examination, best corrected visual acuity assessment (BCVA), slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and fundoscopy, were done for all patients. DR was diagnosed by biomicroscopic fundus examination. Serum survivin level was estimated by enzyme linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) technique and survivin messenger ribonucleic acid (mRNA) expression by quantitative reverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) as potential biomarkers of DR. Serum survivin was significantly increased in DR patients than those without DR (p < 0.01). Serum survivin and its mRNA expression correlated significantly and positively with HbA1c in DM patients (r = 0.808 and 0.618, p < 0.001). Serum survivin has an AUC of 0.985 (95% CI: 0.955 - 1.000, p < 0.001) with a sensitivity of 96.67% and specificity of 93.33% at a cutoff value of >360 pg/mL. For survivin mRNA expression, the AUC was 0.907 (95% CI: 0.820 - 0.995, p < 0.001) with a sensitivity of 86.67 % and specificity of 83.33 % at a cutoff value of >1.7. In conclusion, survivin mRNA expression and its serum level are elevated in patients with DR than those without DR. They showed strong positive correlation with HbA1c level. Both survivin mRNA expression and its serum level might have a marked role in the diagnosis of DR.

title: Automated Two-component Pre-CTPA ECG Risk Phenotype and 365-day Mortality among ECG-evaluated Patients with Computed Tomography-confirmed Pulmonary Embolism.
abstract: Objective Electrocardiographic abnormalities are common in acute pulmonary embolism, but their prognostic value in public waveform-linked cohorts remains incompletely characterized. We evaluated whether an interpretable automated two-component pre-CTPA ECG risk phenotype was associated with 365-day mortality among ECG-evaluated patients with CTPA-confirmed pulmonary embolism. Method This secondary analysis used a retrospective cohort derived from MIMIC-IV-Ext-PE linked to MIMIC-IV-ECG. The source population included 1,534 unique PE-positive patients after patient-level indexing. A total of 650 patients had an ECG within 6 hours before CTPA, 571 were admission-linked, and 567 passed waveform signal-quality screening. The exposure assigned 1 point for tachycardia >100 beats/min and 1 point for V3 T-wave inversion. The primary Cox model was adjusted for age, sex, Charlson comorbidity index, PE subtype, ICU admission initiated at or before CTPA, and early physiologic derangement after excluding heart rate from the derangement definition. Results The primary cohort included 567 patients and 126 deaths within 365 days. Crude 365-day mortality increased across score levels: 15.0% for score 0, 26.8% for score 1, and 41.7% for score 2. In the primary model, each 1-point increase in the score was associated with higher 365-day mortality (HR 1.70 [1.36-2.13], P<0.001). The exposure-level proportional hazards diagnostic did not show clear evidence of violation (P=0.060). A stabilized inverse-probability-of-selection weighted Cox model yielded a similar estimate (HR 1.59, 95% CI 1.28-1.99; P<0.001), although measured selection imbalance was reduced but not eliminated. Conclusion Among ECG-evaluated patients with CTPA-confirmed pulmonary embolism, an automated two-component pre-CTPA ECG risk phenotype was associated with higher 365-day mortality. The phenotype should be interpreted as an early prognostic marker requiring further validation rather than as a validated clinical decision tool.

title: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor of the greater omentum in a 7-year-old girl.
abstract: Inflammatory myofibroblastic tumor is a rare neoplasm. Its preferred location is intrathoracic; there are few reports of intra-abdominal involvement, where it may affect the mesentery and retroperitoneum. A 7-year-old girl was brought in for evaluation due to fever, nonspecific lower abdominal pain, fatigue, and progressive weight loss. Laboratory tests revealed anemia, thrombocytosis, and elevated CRP. An abdominal ultrasound showed a hypoechoic mass with well-defined borders and heterogeneous content, measuring approximately 67 × 52 × 79 mm. Complete excision was performed via laparotomy. Its low incidence, varied location, nonspecific histology, and clinical heterogeneity make diagnosis extremely difficult. Only histopathology allows for a definitive diagnosis, and the cornerstone of treatment remains complete removal of the tumor. This rare condition should be included in the pediatric differential diagnosis because of its nonspecific clinical presentation, intra-abdominal mass, and high recurrence rate after incomplete resection.

title: Interstitial lung disease as the initial manifestation of systemic autoimmune disease: a narrative review of autoantibodies, biomarkers, prognosis, and management.
abstract: Interstitial lung disease (ILD) may be the first or only clinically apparent manifestation of systemic autoimmune rheumatic disease (SARD), preceding extrapulmonary features by months or years. The European Respiratory Society/American Thoracic Society research classification of interstitial pneumonia with autoimmune features (IPAF) provides a framework for patients with interstitial pneumonia and autoimmune features who do not meet criteria for a defined SARD. Importantly, IPAF requires features from at least two of three domains - clinical, serologic, and morphologic - and cannot be assigned on autoantibody positivity alone. Extended, phenotype-directed autoantibody testing can reveal lung-dominant anti-synthetase syndrome, clinically amyopathic dermatomyositis, early systemic sclerosis, rheumatoid arthritis, or Sjögren's syndrome (Autoimmune epithelitis). Prognosis is heterogeneous and is driven more consistently by the fibrotic burden, usual interstitial pneumonia pattern, baseline and longitudinal pulmonary physiology, and comorbidities than by the IPAF label itself. KL-6, surfactant protein D, CCL18, MMP-7, and multiplex proteomic signatures are promising biomarkers, but none is sufficiently validated to replace serial high-resolution computed tomography and pulmonary function testing. Management should be individualised through multidisciplinary discussion. Immunomodulation is most defensible for inflammatory or SARD-like phenotypes, whereas antifibrotic therapy should be considered when progressive pulmonary fibrosis is established despite appropriate management. IPAF should therefore be viewed as a dynamic research phenotype within a continuum of lung-dominant autoimmunity, requiring longitudinal reassessment for evolution to a defined SARD.

title: Lung ultrasound as part of a diagnostic algorithm to detect interstitial lung disease in rheumatoid arthritis patients at risk.
abstract: Objectives Rheumatoid arthritis-associated interstitial lung disease (RA-ILD) affects 5-10% of patients with RA. While lung ultrasound (LUS) shows promise for RA-ILD detection, its role remains inconclusive. We aimed to assess its performance as a screening tool in at-risk RA patients. Methods We made a cross-sectional study of RA patients, including i) individuals >50 years old with ≥1 risk factor for ILD, and ii) patients with new-onset respiratory symptoms. All patients underwent clinical examination, pulmonary function testing (PFT), LUS, and chest high-resolution computed tomography (HRCT). LUS was considered abnormal in case of ≥5 total B-lines, and diagnostic accuracy was compared against HRCT, using a recent American Thoracic Society definition. Results We included 103 RA patients (73% women; mean age 63.4 years, median disease duration 7 years, 62% current or ever smokers, 68% seropositive for RF and/or ACPA). The majority (67 patients, 64.4%) reported no respiratory symptoms and had normal lung auscultation. According to ATS definition, 23 patients (22.3%) had ILD. Use of LUS for RA-ILD showed a sensitivity of 60.9% (95% CI: 40.8-77.8%), specificity of 63.7% (95% CI: 52.8-73.4%), and a negative predictive value (NPV) of 85% (95% CI: 73.9-91.9%). In regression and random forest analyses, LUS did not outperform DLCO for the prediction of RA-ILD. However, combination of negative LUS examination with normal DLCO essentially excluded RA-ILD (NPV 100%, 95%CI: 82-100%). Conclusions Negative LUS in combination with normal DLCO reliably exclude ILD in at-risk RA patients, supporting its role in early RA-ILD detection.

title: Maternal serum biomarkers and early pregnancy Doppler blood flow patterns.
abstract: Objectives This study aimed to evaluate the association between first‑trimester maternal serum biomarkers - β‑hCG, PAPP‑A, sFLT‑1, and PLGF - and Doppler ultrasound indices (uterine arteries and ductus venosus), and to determine their utility in predicting preeclampsia (PE). Material and methods In this prospective study (2021-2022) at University Hospital No. 2, Bydgoszcz, 137 pregnant women in the first trimester (11+0-13+6 weeks) were enrolled. Participants were assigned to an experimental group (n = 86, with PE risk factors) or a control group (n = 51). Serum levels of β‑hCG, PAPP‑A, PLGF, and sFLT‑1 were measured using electrochemiluminescence immunoassay, and Doppler ultrasound was used to assess uterine artery and ductus venosus blood flow. Mean arterial pressure (MAP) was recorded, and PE risk was calculated using FMF software. Results The experimental group had significantly lower PLGF levels (mean MoM 0.864 vs. 1.028, p = 0.0075) and higher sFLT‑1/PLGF ratios (34.32 vs 28.79, p = 0.0280) compared to controls. Additionally, MAP was significantly elevated (86.4 mmHg vs 79.5 mmHg, p < 0.0001) and the ductus venosus pulsatility index was lower (1.00 vs 1.07, p = 0.0132). Spearman analysis showed that increased PE risk correlated with lower PAPP‑A (R = -0.20, p = 0.0201) and PLGF (R = -0.54, p < 0.0001) and with a higher sFLT‑1/PLGF ratio (R = 0.40, p < 0.0001). Conclusions Our findings support the utility of an integrated first‑trimester screening strategy that combines maternal risk factors, biochemical markers (PLGF and PAPP‑A), and biophysical parameters (MAP and Doppler indices) for early identification of pregnancies at elevated risk for PE. This approach may facilitate prophylactic interventions to improve maternal and perinatal outcomes.

title: Anatomical Variations of Renal Arteries: Clinical, Radiological, and Surgical Considerations.
abstract: Objective To synthesize the current knowledge regarding the embryological basis, anatomical classification, imaging characterization, and clinical implications of accessory renal arteries. Background Anatomical variations in the renal arteries are common, affecting approximately 20-35% of the population, and have significant implications for clinical outcomes and surgical planning. Accessory renal arteries are usually terminal vessels that serve discrete renal islands with minimal collateral circulation in the body; therefore, their preoperative identification is important. However, there has been no modern synthesis of embryology, imaging, and multidisciplinary clinical treatment for these variations. Methods A narrative review of the literature was conducted by searching PubMed and Google Scholar for publications from December 2015 to December 2025. MeSH terms and free-text keywords related to "accessory renal artery," "multiple renal arteries," "renal artery variations," "renal vascular anatomy," "kidney transplantation," "renovascular hypertension," "computed tomography angiography," "magnetic resonance angiography," and "endovascular aortic repair" were used in Boolean combinations. Peer-reviewed original studies, systematic reviews, meta-analyses, and case series were included. Conference abstracts, unpublished data, and non-English publications were excluded. Discussion This review addresses the embryological basis and anatomical classification of accessory renal arteries; the diagnostic roles of Doppler ultrasound, computed tomography angiography, and magnetic resonance angiography; and their clinical implications in kidney transplantation, partial nephrectomy, and endovascular aortic repair, including the contested association with renovascular hypertension. Available data suggest that most accessory vessels do not independently cause hypertension, whereas stenosis of larger vessels may be a correctable etiology in selected cases. Conclusion Accessory renal arteries have a significant clinical impact, primarily determined by the size of the vessels and the area of the kidney they supply. Preoperative characterization based on modern imaging can be reliable and can help plan and manage surgery for each patient. More prospective research is required to establish evidence-based principles for vessel maintenance and evaluate new technologies in this context.

title: Angiographically Occult Perforator Ischemia Detected by Motor-Evoked Potential Monitoring during Woven EndoBridge Deployment: A Case Report.
abstract: Objective To demonstrate that intraoperative motor-evoked potential (MEP) monitoring can detect angiographically occult perforator ischemia caused by intermediate catheter-induced luminal occupation and flow restriction during Woven EndoBridge (WEB; Terumo Neuro, Aliso Viejo, CA, USA) deployment, which would otherwise remain unrecognized. Case presentation A woman in her 60s underwent WEB deployment for an unruptured left middle cerebral artery aneurysm under general anesthesia with intraoperative MEP monitoring using an optimized transcranial electrical stimulation protocol. Immediately prior to device deployment, MEP amplitudes abruptly disappeared in the right extremities. DSA showed preserved lenticulostriate artery opacification; however, the M1 segment was nearly completely occupied by the intermediate catheter. Catheter-induced perforator ischemia was suspected, and the catheter was promptly withdrawn to the cavernous internal carotid artery. MEP signals fully recovered within approximately 4 minutes, and WEB deployment was completed without further incident. Postoperative MRI revealed a small lacunar infarction in the lenticulostriate territory, but the patient was discharged without neurological deficits. Conclusion Intermediate catheter-induced luminal occupation of the parent artery can cause angiographically occult perforator ischemia detectable only by functional monitoring. MEP monitoring may serve as a critical safeguard during WEB deployment and other neuroendovascular procedures involving large-bore intermediate catheters in perforator-rich arterial segments.

title: Prehospital point-of-care ultrasound as a decision-support tool: A structured narrative review.
abstract: Background Point-of-care ultrasound (POCUS) may support focused bedside decisions, but prehospital implementation remains limited by operational constraints, heterogeneous protocols, variable training, and limited outcome-focused evidence. This narrative review examines prehospital POCUS as a clinical decision-support tool across cardiac, thoracic, trauma, pediatric, and obstetric applications. Methods A structured narrative review was conducted in MEDLINE/PubMed, Embase, and Cochrane Central from April 2017 to February 2026. Search terms combined the prehospital setting, ultrasound, and clinical applications. Of 464 records identified, 38 full-text articles were included, including nine systematic reviews on cardiac evaluation (n = 2), thoracic evaluation (n = 3), and trauma assessment (n = 4). Screening and full-text assessment were performed by a single reviewer. No formal risk-of-bias assessment, certainty grading, quantitative synthesis, or meta-analysis was performed. Results In cardiac arrest, prehospital POCUS may identify cardiac activity and selected reversible causes, guide interventions, confirm return of spontaneous circulation, and support prognostic assessment, provided that image acquisition does not interrupt resuscitation or delay defibrillation. In nontraumatic shock and cardiac dysfunction, focused cardiac, lung, and vascular ultrasound may help characterize shock mechanisms, guide fluid therapy, and identify actionable findings such as pulmonary congestion, pericardial effusion, right ventricular strain, or major aortic pathology. In acute dyspnea, lung ultrasound may improve diagnostic confidence, particularly for cardiogenic pulmonary edema. In trauma, E-FAST has high specificity and may support triage, destination choice, trauma pathway activation, and preparation for definitive care; however, limited sensitivity prevents its use as a rule-out test. Pediatric and obstetric applications are feasible but remain emerging. Conclusions Prehospital POCUS is an adjunctive decision-support tool rather than a standalone diagnostic test. Its value lies in answering actionable questions that may influence treatment, triage, transport destination, hospital prealert, or pathway activation. Implementation requires protocols, training, quality assurance, and governance, and must not delay time-critical care or transport.

Implementation requires protocols, training, quality assurance, and governance, and must not delay time-critical care or transport.

title: Tomographic ultrasound (tUS) for thyroid volume determination.
abstract: Background Accurate thyroid volume determination is essential for treatment planning. This feasibility study evaluated the accuracy of a novel tomographic ultrasound (tUS) approach compared to 2D ultrasound, using contrast-enhanced computed tomography (ceCT) as reference standard. Methods In this prospective, single-center study, 50 patients undergoing neck ceCT were enrolled. Thyroid volume was measured by 2D ultrasound (ellipsoid model), automatedvolume (tUS uncorrected), physician-corrected volume (tUS corrected) and ceCT. Linear regression for proportional bias, log-transformed Bland-Altman analysis, clinical error metrics and correction duration were evaluated. Results 2D ultrasound showed significant proportional bias (slope=-0.215, p<0.0001) and systematic underestimation (mean difference -6.0mL; geometric mean ratio 0.76). Corrected tUS eliminated proportional bias (p=0.0557) and reduced bias (mean difference +0.8mL; geometric mean ratio 1.04). Corrected tUS achieved lower MAE (4.42mL vs. 6.53mL) and MAPE (19.4% vs. 25.4%) than 2D ultrasound, placing 60.0% vs. 34.0% of cases within ±20% error limits. In enlarged glands (n=19), corrected tUS maintained superior accuracy (MAE 5.82mL, MAPE 12.4%) versus 2D ultrasound (MAE 11.35mL, MAPE 26.5%). Physician correction averaged 2:51minutes, independent of thyroid volume (r=-0.081, p=0.5784). Conclusions In this feasibility study, physician-corrected tUS reduced the size-dependent systematic underestimation observed with 2D ultrasound and yielded volumes closer to ceCT, particularly in enlarged glands, within a clinically feasible workflow. Because the best-performing method required manual expert correction and the limits of agreement with ceCT exceeded the predefined clinical threshold, corrected tUS should be regarded as a promising semi-automated approach that requires further validation, including interobserver assessment, before it can be considered interchangeable with ceCT.

title: Imaging Manifestations and Clinical Analysis of 12 Cases of Anorectal Malignant Melanoma.
abstract: Aim To investigate the computed tomography (CT) and magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) features and clinical characteristics of primary anorectal malignant melanoma (ARMM). Methods This retrospective analysis was conducted on the clinical, imaging and pathological data of 12 patients with pathologically confirmed ARMM admitted to The First Affiliated Hospital, Zhejiang University School of Medicine between March 2021 and December 2024, and the relevant literature was reviewed and summarized. Results All patients underwent CT and MRI examinations. Among the 12 patients, 5 were male and 7 were female; their ages ranged from 37 to 78 years, with a median age of 65 years. The clinical manifestations were diverse, with bloody stool being the most common (58.3%), followed by anal pain (16.7%) and polypoid vegetation prolapsing from the anus (16.7%). Typical anal pigmentation with pruritus was rare (8.3%). Gross pathological examination revealed a polypoid tumor in 7 cases and an ulcerative or infiltrative growth pattern in 5 cases. Immunohistochemical staining results showed that 12 cases were positive for human melanoma black-45 (HMB-45) and Melan-A, and 9 cases were positive for S-100. On imaging, plain CT scan showed that the tumors were predominantly isodense or slightly hyperdense, with a maximum diameter of approximately 2-5 cm. The enhancement patterns varied, but the tumors predominantly demonstrated marked heterogeneous enhancement. On MRI, most lesions were isointense on T1WI (10/12); 11/12 lesions were slightly hyperintense on T2WI, and hyperintense on diffusion-weighted images (DWI). After enhancement, most tumors exhibited marked heterogeneous enhancement. Conclusions Most of the ARMM lesions in this group demonstrated atypical MRI signal characteristics, making diagnosis challenging. When an anorectal tumor exhibits iso- or hypointensity on T1WI and hyperintensity on T2WI, ARMM should be considered in the differential diagnosis. The CT manifestations lack specificity, and clinical symptoms may mimic those of benign lesions. ARMM may show involvement of the perirectal fat plane on imaging and regional lymph node metastasis and generally shows limited sensitivity to radiotherapy and chemotherapy, contributing to low therapeutic efficacy and poor prognosis. The definitive diagnosis of ARMM depends on histopathological examination, with immunohistochemical staining for S-100, HMB-45 and Melan-A can provide supportive information for the diagnosis of ARMM.

title: Evaluating the Interplay and Impact of Quality and Technical Variations on Performance of AI Models in Multi-Institutional Prostate MRI Datasets
abstract: PurposeTo evaluate whether visually assessed high-quality prostate MRI, as defined by the Prostate Imaging Quality (PI-QUAL) scoring system, is sufficient to ensure consistent AI model performance, or whether hidden acquisition-related technical effects introduce variability that cannot be detected through visual inspection. MethodsThis retrospective study included 568 bpMRI scans from seven institutions, classified using PI-QUAL v2 into high-quality (scores 2-3) and low-quality (score 1) groups. Quantitative image quality features were extracted using MRQy from T2w and ADC sequences. Three experiments were conducted on high-quality scans: (1) unsupervised clustering to identify hidden technical batch effects; (2) V-Net models (M) for prostate capsule segmentation on T2w using single-cluster and balanced multi-cluster training strategies; and (3) VoxelMorph-based deformable registration (M2) to align ADC maps to T2w images. Performance metrics included DSC, precision, recall, volume ratio, HD95, ASSD, and TRE. Kruskal-Wallis tests assessed cross-cluster variability, Two One-Sided Tests (TOST) evaluated performance equivalence, and bootstrap resampling quantified training efficiency. ResultsClustering identified four clusters among 277 high-quality bpMRI scans. Single-cluster models showed variable performance (DSC=0.41-0.85) with significant batch effects (p<0.001), even with 140 training samples. The balanced multi-cluster model (n=60) eliminated batch effects (p=0.075), achieved equivalent performance (p<0.001), and demonstrated 2.23-fold greater training efficiency despite using 2.3-fold fewer samples. Registration performance also varied significantly across clusters (TRE=0.86-5.47 mm, p<0.001). ConclusionAcquisition-related batch effects significantly impact AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among high-quality scans. Quantitative clustering enables detection of technical variations and supports diversity-aware training strategies that achieve equivalent performance with 2.3-fold fewer samples while eliminating batch effects. SummaryAcquisition-related batch effects significantly impair AI generalizability in prostate MRI, even among scans meeting PI-QUAL quality standards. Clustering-based diversity-aware training strategies successfully eliminated these batch effects and achieved 2.23-fold greater training efficiency compared to single-site approaches, demonstrating that strategic technical diversity outweighs dataset size for developing robust, clinically deployable AI models. C_LIO_LIEven the model trained on the largest single cluster exhibited significant batch effects (p<0.001). In contrast, a balanced multi-cluster model eliminated cross-cluster variability (p=0.075) while maintaining equivalent performance and requiring a smaller sample size. C_LIO_LIDiversity-aware training achieved 2.23-fold greater training efficiency (95% CI: 2.18-2.29) with 2.3-fold fewer samples, demonstrating that technical diversity outweighs data quantity for robust AI generalization. C_LI Clinical relevanceAddressing batch effects is essential for developing reliable, generalizable AI tools for prostate MRI interpretation.

title: Deep Learning Trained Without Target-Domain Labels Improves Risk Stratification Over Expert Coronary Calcium Reading on Routine Attenuation Correction CT
abstract: Coronary artery calcium (CAC) is an established measure of coronary atherosclerosis on computed tomography (CT). Many SPECT and most PET myocardial perfusion studies already include a low-dose CT scan from which coronary calcium could be reported, yet it almost never is. CAC may not be reported due to image noise, cardiac motion, or the absence of a reliable reference standard. Deep learning (DL) models trained on these low-dose CT scans inherit the same uncertainty, because their reference labels are drawn on the degraded images. We bypassed this limitation by training a DL CAC model entirely outside the target domain: expert labels from high-quality gated CT were inherited by synthetic ungated images derived from those same scans, so that no CTAC scan was annotated, and no real CTAC image was used, at any point in training. Models were trained using one center and externally tested in two other centers. Because each synthetic image is derived from the gated scan itself, expert gated segmentations remain valid voxel-for-voxel without registration. Using these pairs, we developed a cross-domain knowledge adaptation model (knowledge adaptation, KAD-CAC). The DL models were externally tested on 5969 patients with a median age of 64 (IQR 56 - 73), of whom 50.2% were male. The KAD-CAC model had higher Cohens kappa K (0.86, 95% CI 0.84 - 0.88) compared to a convolutional LSTM model (K 0.78, 95% CI 0.76 - 0.80, p<0.01), or models trained with only gated images (K 0.81, 95% CI 0.80 - 0.82, p<0.01). Net reclassification improvement for death or myocardial infarction over a clinical and perfusion baseline was greatest for the KAD-CAC model and exceeded that of expert CAC reading on the same CTAC scans (difference 0.089, 95% CI 0.051 to 0.125, p<0.001). A model trained without any labels from CTAC scans therefore stratified risk of death or MI better than expert reading of the same scans. Patients classified as CAC 0 by KAD-CAC had lower adjusted risk of death or MI than patients classified as CAC 0 by experts (HR 0.50, 95% CI 0.25 - 0.98). We use paired synthetic ungated scans to transfer expert gated CAC annotations into the ungated domain, resulting in better vessel-level CAC scoring and improved risk reclassification compared with expert reading of the same scans. Automated CAC scoring could be added to every myocardial perfusion imaging report without additional imaging or radiation. The approach provides a general route to expert-quality supervision for any acquisition in which the native reference standard is unreliable.

title: FreqFuseNet: Scale-Normalized Dual-Frequency Fusion for Thin-Wall Head-and-Neck OAR Segmentation
abstract: Accurate segmentation of thin-wall organs-at-risk (OARs) in head-and-neck computed tomography (CT) is challenging because small contour deviations can substantially affect boundary agreement. We present FreqFuseNet, a segmentation architecture with a fast Fourier transform (FFT) primary branch and a frequency channel attention network (FcaNet) residual branch that explicitly aligns heterogeneous frequency-feature scales before bounded residual fusion. An initialization-time analysis revealed an approximately 863-fold activation-scale disparity between the two branches, corresponding to an approximately 43-fold unintended residual-to-primary magnitude ratio under naive fusion with a nominal coefficient of 0.05. FreqFuseNet uses per-sample, per-channel scale alignment to preserve the intended relative amplitude without additional normalization parameters. We evaluated 10 thin-wall OARs on SegRap2023 (84 training, 18 validation, and 18 testing CT cases) under a standardized binary per-OAR region-of-interest (ROI) protocol. In two training seeds, FreqFuseNet achieved Dice of 0.849 and 0.843, 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) of 0.824 and 0.823 mm, and surface Dice at 1 mm of 0.959 and 0.957. In case-level paired comparisons for the primary seed (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, not corrected for multiple comparisons), FreqFuseNet showed significant improvements over 3D U-Net and MedNeXt-S, whereas differences versus an alternative learned fusion design (FixedFusion) and SegResNet were not statistically significant. These findings identify a practical feature-scale calibration issue in dual-frequency segmentation and demonstrate competitive boundary-sensitive performance of the proposed architecture within the evaluated ROI-based setting.

title: Benchmarking Open-Source Vision-Language Models for Brain Metastasis Assessment on Single-Slice Contrast-Enhanced MRI
abstract: PurposeOpen-source vision-language models (VLMs) can be locally deployed without external internet access. This study aimed to evaluate the slice-level lesion-detection performance of multiple general-purpose and medical-purpose open-source VLMs for brain metastases on contrast-enhanced (CE) MRI, and to assess their accuracy in characterizing detailed imaging features on lesion-positive images. Materials and MethodsOne hundred lesion-positive axial CE T1-weighted images and 100 matched lesion-negative images from 100 patients were analyzed using eight evaluable VLMs: five general-purpose VLMs-InternVL3-8B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B-Instruct, MiniCPM-V-4.5, DeepSeek-VL2-tiny, and Phi-3.5-vision-instruct-and three medical-purpose VLMs-MedGemma-4B-it, LLaVA-Med v1.5, and HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B. Lesion-detection performance was assessed using sensitivity, specificity, and balanced accuracy. On lesion-positive images, accuracy was evaluated for lesion count, laterality, anatomic location, enhancement pattern, necrosis, and mass effect. Balanced accuracy was reported with patient-level cluster bootstrap 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Models were compared using the Friedman test and paired patient-level permutation tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction. Secondary outcomes were compared with majority-class baselines using exact McNemar tests. A revised prompt was tested post hoc. ResultsThe median age of the study patients was 65 years (IQR, 59.0-70.0), and 58 patients were male (58.0%). MiniCPM-V-4.5 showed significantly higher balanced accuracy (80.5%; 95% CI, 75.0-85.5) than all other models (FDR-adjusted P < 0.001). Seven of the eight models showed predicted-positive rates of 81-100%, and 70.8% (17/24) of responses to synthetic control images without anatomic content were classified as lesion-positive. With the revised prompt, balanced accuracy increased from 59.5% to 77.0% in HuatuoGPT-Vision-7B and from 51.5% to 68.5% in InternVL3-8B. No model significantly outperformed the majority-class baseline for enhancement pattern or for mass effect. ConclusionThis slice-level technical benchmark demonstrated variable lesion-detection performance of open-source VLMs for brain metastasis in an image-only setting, with most models showing a strong positive-response tendency.

title: Functional connectivity correlates of post-acute covid 19 cognitive and neuropsychiatric complications
abstract: Background The neuropsychiatric sequelae (cognitive deficits, anxiety and depression) post-COVID-19 exist as part of the spectrum of the multisystemic long COVID. People with these symptoms have been shown to have worse functional outcomes. Hence, this significantly impacts the economy, primarily due to productivity losses. Yet, the precise underlying pathogenesis remains unknown, as do any diagnostic or prognostic biomarkers. Aim This study aims to identify functionally impacted brain regions in those with post-COVID-19 neurological sequelae and to evaluate how alterations in brain function relate to acute serum inflammatory mediators and brain injury biomarkers. Methods The study will utilise data from the COVID-19 Clinical Neuroscience Study (CNS), a large UK multicentre study conducted during the pandemic. This sub-study will be a secondary analysis of the COVID-19 CNS, a prospective observational study that compared COVID-19-positive participants with negative controls. Participants had an MRI, blood tested for acute serum inflammatory mediators and brain injury biomarkers, and neuropsychiatric assessment (cognitron test, PHQ-9 and GAD-7) post-acutely and at follow-up. The DPABI (Data Processing & Analysis for Brain Imaging) toolbox will be used for pre-processing and analysis of the neuroimaging data (resting state functional MRI) to obtain regional homogeneity (ReHo). The association between ReHO and neuropsychiatric symptoms, acute inflammatory mediators and brain injury biomarkers will be explored. Regression models would be used to determine the risk and protective factors for developing these symptoms. Conclusion It is anticipated that the study will provide new insights into the functional basis of post-acute COVID-19 neuropsychiatric manifestations and identify new diagnostic biomarkers.

title: Clinical and Radiomics Predictors of Post-stroke Longitudinal Mortality: A Prospective Cohort Study from a Tertiary Care Hospital in India
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Stroke imposes substantial mortality and socioeconomic burden in India, particularly among younger adults. However, prospective evidence on the prognostic value of baseline clinical and radiomics features for mortality prediction remains limited. Objective To assess mortality at 28, 90, 180, and 365 days after stroke; characterize survival patterns across stroke subtypes and vascular territories; and identify baseline demographic, clinical, and radiomics predictors of mortality. Methods This prospective cohort study recruited consecutive patients with stroke admitted to a tertiary care hospital in Mangalore, India. Demographic, clinical, laboratory, and radiomics features were collected at admission, and mortality was assessed at 28, 90, 180, and 365 days. Kaplan–Meier analysis was used to compare survival across stroke subtypes and vascular territories, while Cox proportional hazards regression was used to identify independent baseline predictors of mortality. Results Among 63 confirmed stroke cases, 38 (60%) had ischemic stroke (IS) and 25 (40%) had haemorrhagic stroke (HS). Within the middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, HS patients demonstrated better survival than IS patients due to a greater burden of adverse baseline characteristics such as previous stroke, atrial fibrillation, and higher lesion volume in the IS-MCA subgroup. The combined clinical-radiomics model demonstrated superior prognostic performance than individual models, with higher concordance indices and consistently lower Akaike Information Criterion values. In the combined model, stroke severity (aHR = 2.35, 3.0, 2.93, 2.41) and DWI texture heterogeneity of lesion (aHR = 2.35, 2.11, 2.24, 2.10) were the strongest predictors of mortality across all time points. The CT attenuation heterogeneity (aHR = 1.81, 28 days; 1.76, 90 days; 1.80, 180 days) of lesion and age (aHR = 1.48, 365 days) were also significant predictors. Conclusion The radiomics features provide critical complementary information to clinical parameters for predicting 28-day mortality, unlike during mid- to long-term follow-up where their incremental contribution appears to be limited. Our results may have important implications in resource-constrained settings for supporting personalized post-stroke management and rehabilitation.

Within the middle cerebral artery (MCA) territory, HS patients demonstrated better survival than IS patients due to a greater burden of adverse baseline characteristics such as previous stroke, atrial fibrillation, and higher lesion volume in the IS-MCA subgroup. Conclusion

The radiomics features provide critical complementary information to clinical parameters for predicting 28-day mortality, unlike during mid- to long-term follow-up where their incremental contribution appears to be limited. Our results may have important implications in resource-constrained settings for supporting personalized post-stroke management and rehabilitation.

title: Pixel-Level Quantification of Subcutaneous Shear-Wave Velocity Heterogeneity for Grading Lymphatic Obstruction in Breast Cancer-Related Lymphedema
abstract: ObjectivesTo develop and validate pixel data analysis (PDA) for reconstructing pixel-level shear-wave velocity (SWV) from saved Holder-Optimized Elastography (HOE) elastograms and to determine whether whole-field subcutaneous heterogeneity provides a quantitative signature of lymphatic obstruction compared with visual high-velocity-area (HVA) counting and sparse manual region-of-interest (ROI) sampling. Materials and MethodsIn this cross-sectional study, 110 women after breast cancer surgery underwent lymphoscintigraphy and HOE, a pressure-minimized acquisition framework that preserves conventionally captured SWV information while additionally revealing spatial abnormalities attenuated by handheld acquisition. Reconstruction validation used 200 paired ROIs, spanning nearly the full displayed SWV range, from 49 images retrieved from the picture archiving and communication system; reproducibility was assessed across 96 matched anatomical sites from 6 participants undergoing independently reacquired HOE examinations. PDA, visual HVA counting, and manual ROI sampling were evaluated on the same HOE-acquired elastograms in task-specific common complete-case cohorts. ResultsPDA reconstructed the machine-reported SWV with near-zero error over a range of 1.17 - 9.97 m/s (mean difference, +0.0009 m/s; mean absolute error, 0.0075 m/s; 95% limits of agreement, -0.0202 to +0.0221 m/s). For subcutaneous variance, interobserver/intraobserver intraclass correlation coefficients were 0.709/0.799 for PDA and 0.178/0.560 for manual ROI sampling. In the primary no obstruction versus partial obstruction comparison (n = 93), forearm-pooled PDA subcutaneous variance ratio yielded the highest observed area under the curve (AUC, 0.858; 95% confidence interval, 0.771 - 0.946), compared with 0.820 for visual HVA counting and 0.794 for manual ROI sampling. PDAs subcutaneous variance ratio remained a leading feature across all three comparisons (AUC, 0.858 - 0.878), including partial versus total obstruction grading, where all three frameworks showed high discrimination. ConclusionsPDA accurately reconstructs pixel-level SWV from saved HOE elastograms and enables reproducible whole-field quantification of superficial shear-wave elastography heterogeneity. Subcutaneous variance ratio was the leading quantitative PDA feature across lymphatic-obstruction comparisons and was particularly informative in partial obstruction. The same approach also enables retrospective quantitative reanalysis of compatible archived elastograms. Plain-Language SummaryPixel data analysis (PDA) reconstructs quantitative pixel-level shear-wave velocity from saved superficial elastography images, allowing the complete measurable color field to be analyzed rather than a few manually sampled regions. Reconstructed values closely matched machine measurements, and whole-field subcutaneous variance was substantially more reproducible than manual ROI sampling. Subcutaneous variance ratio remained a leading diagnostic signal across obstruction severities, including in partial obstruction without visually detectable high-velocity areas.

title: High-SNR Whole-Brain Mesoscale Diffusion MRI Using Rotating-View Acquisitions (ROVER-dMRI)
abstract: Purpose We aim to acquire and reconstruct high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), whole-brain, mesoscale (isotropic submillimeter) diffusion MRI (dMRI) in vivo in a clinically feasible scan time. Methods We present ROVER-dMRI, a unified rotating-view acquisition and super-resolution reconstruction framework. Thick slices (up to 10 mm) acquired across many rotated orientations improve the base SNR, and a shared multi-resolution hash-encoded implicit neural representation (INR) with per-direction MLP head and a physics-informed, Bloch-simulated slice-profile forward model reconstructs these views into a continuous isotropic volume (up to 13× super-resolution) in a self-supervised manner. ROVER-dMRI was evaluated in vivo on human brain (0.78 mm isotropic and 0.5 mm isotropic) and monkey brain (0.6 mm isotropic) across MRI platforms with varying gradient performance, and benchmarked against gSlider-SMS and least-squares super-resolution reconstruction (LS-SRR). Results At 0.78 mm isotropic resolution, ROVER-dMRI diffusion-weighted images achieved higher SNR than the vendor product sequence, whose images were limited by the noise floor, while its directionally encoded color (DEC) maps showed lower noise than gSlider. When reducing the number of views from 20 to 13 (reducing the scan time by 65%), ROVER-dMRI acquisition/reconstruction preserved all fine details in the fiber orientations. In the monkey brain, its DEC map matched a 60-direction gSlider acquisition at only 40% of the scan time. ROVER-dMRI preserved coherent fiber-orientation-distribution (FOD) structure, including crossing fibers, and recovered fine details in the cerebellum at 0.5 mm isotropic, that are not visible at 0.78 mm resolution. Compared to state-of-the-art 0.5 mm methods, ROVER-dMRI reduced scan time by 73% while acquiring more diffusion directions. Conclusion ROVER-dMRI offers a practical route to high-SNR whole-brain mesoscale diffusion imaging in vivo, with the pulse sequence and reconstruction pipeline released as open source.

title: AREION: A Foundation Model for Atlas-Agnostic Representation Learning of Brain Connectome
abstract: Brain foundation models have shown promising advances in learning generalizable representations from functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) data. However, existing models are typically tied to specific brain atlases and cannot be applied to fMRI data represented using different atlases without full retraining, thereby severely limiting their broader utility across neuroimaging studies. To address this bottleneck, we introduce AREION, atlas-agnostic representation learning of brain connectomes. AREION overcomes atlas dependency through two integrated innovations. First, a Brain Region Contextualizing technique maps brain regions and connectivity entries from diverse atlases into a unified representation space based on their spatial, functional, and morphological characteristics. Second, a Hierarchical Brain Transformer Encoder processes region-specific connectivity profiles as variable-length token sequences and jointly captures local functional structure and global brain functional organization, conditioned on brain regional context, without assuming a fixed number of regions. Together, these two techniques enable the learning of generalizable representations across brain atlases with different parcellation resolutions and connectivity dimensions. AREION is pretrained on a large-scale multi-atlas cohort of fMRI data via self-supervised modeling and evaluated across diverse downstream tasks. Extensive experiments show that it outperforms strong supervised baselines and fMRI foundation models while using substantially fewer parameters, demonstrating strong transferability to atlases unseen during pretraining, generalization to external datasets, and excellent interpretability at the brain regional level.

title: A cascade of attentional and default mode network dynamics following the resolution of perceptual ambiguity
abstract: The neural mechanisms underlying spontaneous perceptual switches during bistable perception, particularly the dynamic interplay between large-scale brain networks, remain incompletely understood. Here, using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) in six participants and a bistable kinetic depth effect (KDE) stimulus, we investigated the spatiotemporal dynamics of brain activity associated with spontaneous perceptual reversals compared to physically induced (replayed) switches. Leveraging a fine-grained functional brain parcellation (MD758) and time-resolved analysis including noise correlations, we identified a distributed network encompassing occipital (MT/MST, LOC), parietal (IPS), and frontal (FEF, IFC, DLPFC) regions showing differential activity during spontaneous versus replayed switches. This network topography qualitatively overlapped a prior review-derived synthesis of perceptual-switching regions. Temporal decomposition of the differential fMRI signal further revealed a characteristic network cascade after the perceptual report: positive dorsal attention (DAN) and visual (VIS) network contrasts peaked approximately 4 s after the report alongside a negative default mode network (DMN) contrast; a slower, more modest ventral attention (VAN)–frontoparietal (FPN) component was observed around 10 s post-report but was weak and is treated as preliminary. The early 4 s profile was recovered across raw-signal, PCA-denoised, and noise-correlation analyses—three related, not fully independent analyses—with the noise-correlation analysis indicating that it is not fully attributable to shared motor-report signals. These findings delineate the temporal sequence of network recruitment following spontaneous perceptual transitions and suggest that interplay between attentional control and default mode networks accompanies the resolution of perceptual ambiguity. Highlights Distributed cortical cascade of network engagement follows spontaneous bistable KDE perceptual switching. Positive DAN–VIS and negative DMN network contrasts peak 4 s post-report. A preliminary, slower VAN–FPN component is observed around 10 s post-report. Noise-correlation analysis indicates the early network profile is not fully explained by shared motor-report signals. Findings: temporally dissect the review-derived BRAS network of bistable perception.

title: Data-Efficient Prostate Micro-Ultrasound Image Analysis using a Modality-specific Foundation Model
abstract: Background and ObjectiveMicro-ultrasound (MicroUS) is an emerging high-resolution imaging modality for prostate cancer diagnosis and real-time biopsy guidance, but its automated analysis is limited by labor-intensive expert annotation. We aimed to develop and evaluate a foundation model for data-efficient MicroUS image analysis. MethodsWe developed {micro}FM, a MicroUS-specific foundation model pretrained using DINOv2-style self-supervised learning on 1,736,391 unlabeled images from 780 patients. The model was fine-tuned and evaluated in three downstream cohorts for prostate capsule segmentation (public, 75 patients), urethra segmentation (institutional, 105 patients), and prostate cancer lesion localization (institutional, 190 patients). Under limited annotation, {micro}FM was compared with randomly initialized models and foundation models pretrained on natural, medical, and ultrasound images. Evaluation used the Dice scores and 95th-percentile Hausdorff distance (HD95) for segmentation and free-response receiver operating characteristic analysis for lesion localization. Key Findings and Limitations{micro}FM improved performance across all three tasks, with the largest gains under limited annotation. With 10% of training scans, {micro}FM achieved Dice scores of 93.8% for prostate capsule segmentation and 58.4% for urethra segmentation, versus 87.9% and 47.0% for the strongest comparators. Corresponding HD95 values were 2.0 and 4.3 mm. For lesion localization, {micro}FM outperformed other models with approximately 0.75 sensitivity at two false-positive detections per 3D volume. Limitations include retrospective single-institution pretraining and lack of explicit 3D modeling. Conclusions and Clinical ImplicationsMicroUS-specific self-supervised pretraining improved data-efficient image analysis across prostate and urethra segmentation, and lesion localization. This approach may reduce annotation requirements for developing automated tools in MicroUS image analysis. Advancing PracticeO_ST_ABSWhat does the study add?C_ST_ABSThis study evaluates a deep learning model pretrained on a large-scale dataset of unlabeled prostate MicroUS images. The pretrained model was adapted to three clinically relevant image-analysis tasks: prostate capsule segmentation, urethra segmentation, and prostate cancer lesion localization. Substantial performance gains over other models were observed despite limited training data, suggesting that MicroUS-specific self-supervised pretraining may reduce expert annotation requirements for developing automated image-analysis tools. Patient SummaryWe developed a foundation model that learns from unlabeled prostate MicroUS images. It performed better with limited labeled data but requires independent validation before clinical use.

title: Continuous Rod Noise and Nonlinear Synaptic Filtering Shape Signal Detection in the Primary Rod Pathway
abstract: Rod photoreceptors are optimized to detect single photons, but their performance near absolute visual threshold is limited by intrinsic phototransduction noise. The two major components are discrete single-photon-like events and continuous fluctuations in outer-segment current. Although spontaneous rhodopsin activation is established as the source of discrete noise, the molecular origin of continuous noise remains controversial, and how these distinct noise sources influence signal processing at the first visual synapse is not fully understood. To address these questions, we combined genetic manipulation of rhodopsin, phosphodiesterase 6 (PDE6), and glutamic acid rich protein 2 (GARP2) with single-cell recordings from rods and rod-bipolar cells (RBCs) and pharmacological manipulation of mGluR6 signaling. Continuous noise was unaffected by reduced rhodopsin concentration but was strongly influenced by PDE6 expression and regulation, supporting basal PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise. Reducing either discrete or continuous noise increased signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) in rods, but these changes were differentially processed at the rod-to-RBC synapse. In WT retina, the nonlinear transformation increased SNR, whereas elevated continuous noise limited this increase. Conversely, reduced continuous noise increased rod SNR, which was maintained in RBCs and associated with a lower detection threshold. Pharmacological reduction of the mGluR6-dependent nonlinearity altered these genotype-dependent differences, indicating that nonlinear filtering is well matched to normal signal and noise distributions but does not fully compensate when presynaptic noise is experimentally altered. Together, our study identifies spontaneous PDE6 activity as a major source of continuous noise and demonstrates that continuous noise interacts with nonlinear processing at the first visual synapse to determine the fidelity and detection threshold of dim-light signals. Significance Statement Vision near absolute threshold requires retinal circuits to distinguish single-photon responses from intrinsic photoreceptor noise. We show that basal PDE6 activity is a major source of continuous noise in rod photoreceptors and that altering this noise affects signal fidelity after convergence onto rod bipolar cells. Nonlinear filtering at the first visual synapse interacts with presynaptic noise levels, while reducing continuous rod noise improves the detection of near-threshold light signals. These findings link the molecular mechanisms generating photoreceptor noise to its processing by downstream retinal circuitry and demonstrate how noise control at both cellular and synaptic levels contributes to the remarkable sensitivity of the primary rod pathway.

title: Age-Adjusted Cerebellar Volumetry and Developmental Outcomes in Extremely Low Birth Weight Infants
abstract: Background Infants with extremely low birth weight (ELBW) are at high risk for neurodevelopmental impairment, but the relationship between cerebellar structure and later developmental outcome remains incompletely defined. Methods In this retrospective single-center study, we examined total cerebellar volume on clinically acquired brain magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) in ELBW infants while accounting for postmenstrual age (PMA) at imaging. Results Of 65 infants screened, 42 were included. Mean gestational age at birth was 25.54 ± 1.68 weeks, mean birth weight was 733.2 ± 118.7 g, and mean PMA at MRI was 43.02 ± 6.53 weeks (range, 31.57–68.00). Mean cerebellar volume was 22.17 ± 9.63 cm 3 . Independently adjudicated developmental outcomes comprised normal development in 16 infants, isolated or specific impairment in 12, and moderate/severe impairment in 14. Unadjusted cerebellar volumes did not differ across developmental groups (P = 0.490) or qualitative MRI categories (P = 0.875). However, the PMA-by-developmental-category interaction was significant (P = 0.002), with estimated cross-sectional slopes of 1.72, 1.56, and 0.39 cm 3 per week, respectively. The interaction remained significant within 36–46 weeks PMA (n = 29; P = 0.011) and after adjustment for small-for-gestational-age status. Sensitivity analyses indicated uncertainty in the stability of the interaction. Conclusions These findings suggest that age-informed cerebellar volumetric patterns may provide developmental information not evident from average volumes alone and support prospective validation with standardized imaging and developmental assessments. As a result, cerebellar volumes obtained early in life may hold prognostic information for ELBW infants.
