title: Optogenetic and sonogenetic pacing of unmodified cardiac tissue upon quick integration with specialized biological actuators
abstract: ABSTRACT Electrical stimulation for cardiac pacing has been in clinical use for 100 years and it is the current standard. Alternative scalable pacing methods that are contactless, with good spatial precision and can also be cell-selective are of interest for both in vitro and in vivo applications. Cardiac pacing by light or by ultrasound (US) can be achieved using optogenetic transduction of the tissue and by enhancing responsiveness to ultrasound. In this work we create specialized biological actuators (cell spheroids) out of generic human cells, modified optogenetically (using Channelrhodopsin2) and sonogenetically (using human Piezo1), guide them to a desired location to promote quick integration with unmodified cardiac syncytia within less than two hours. We quantify their ability to confer pacing by light or US and to entrain the native cardiac tissue, modeled here with human induced pluripotent stem cell derived cardiomyocytes (hiPSC-CMs) grown in monolayers, quasi-3D oriented microtissues or cell spheroids. Magnetic guidance (via magnetic nanoparticles) speeds up integration and facilitates positioning to optimize electrotonic load for pacing; size match and three-dimensional growth also accelerate integration. Computational modeling corroborates the possibility to pace by light and by US. Using optogenetically-gated US pulses (0.5 MHz), we show entrainment in voltage and calcium responses and identify the best performing configurations. Experiments reveal the potential role of Piezo1, esp. when activated with Yoda1. The approach is shown to work with physiologically relevant heart cells, such as human cardiac fibroblasts as optimized actuators, and therefore can be considered for in vivo applications as part of heart regeneration efforts. High-throughput cardiotoxicity testing and drug screening in vitro can directly benefit from deployment of such biological actuators.

title: Ordinal Multi-Instance Learning for Automated Multi-Task Grading of Lumbar Degenerative Conditions on Sagittal MRI, with External Validation
abstract: Purpose: Lumbar spine MRI interpretation requires 25 structured severity judgments per examination (five degenerative conditions at five disc levels, each on a three-level ordinal scale), a time-consuming task with substantial inter-reader variability. We developed and externally validated a model that automates this complete scheme. Materials and Methods: A full-sequence multi-instance learning (MIL) model (ResNet34 backbone, bidirectional GRU, attention pooling over 24 uniformly sampled sagittal T2-weighted slices) with 25 cumulative-logit ordinal heads was trained on 1,204 examinations from the multi-institutional RSNA 2024 LumbarDISC dataset and internally validated on 213 held-out examinations. External validation used 60 retrospectively collected patients from an independent Chinese university hospital (four scanner vendors, radiology reports as the reference standard, no fine-tuning). Agreement was assessed with exact accuracy, sensitivity, specificity, McNemar tests, and patient-clustered bootstrap confidence intervals. Results: The ordinal model achieved 51.4% balanced accuracy internally (exact accuracy 65.1%), versus 16.3% for a single-slice baseline; severe-grade AUCs averaged 0.908 across conditions. Externally, it outperformed its softmax-weighted counterpart on exact accuracy (0.649 vs. 0.586; +6.3 percentage points, 95% CI +2.7 to +10.0) and sensitivity (0.868 vs. 0.833), with markedly fewer severe-grade false alarms (69 vs. 172 predicted severe cells; McNemar p<0.0001). Conclusion: A full-sequence MIL model with ordinal outputs automates the complete 25-task grading scheme on sagittal MRI and, in the first hospital external validation of such a model, reduced severe-grade over-prediction under domain shift without loss of sensitivity, supporting its role as a screening and triage aid.

title: Proximal sesamoid bone fatigue in Thoroughbred racehorses is associated with palmar osteochondral disease in the adjacent third metacarpal bone condyle
abstract: Abstract Background: Proximal sesamoid bone (PSB) stress fracture is a common catastrophic injury in racing Thoroughbreds that is associated with bone sclerosis and development of focal osteolysis. Standing computed tomography (sCT) enables sensitive identification of these structural changes and associations with other more common fetlock fatigue injury such as palmar/plantar osteochondral disease lesions affecting the condyles of the third metacarpal/metatarsal (MC3/MT3). Objective: To gain insight into the PSB stress fracture mechanism, we examined associations between fatigue injury prevalence in the three major metacarpophalangeal (MCP) sites: PSB, parasagittal grooves (PSG), and third metacarpal bone MC3 condyles. Study design: Retrospective clinical study. Methods: We studied 22 catastrophically injured Thoroughbred racehorses. Thoracic limbs were examined using computed tomography (CT) (n=29). Subjective CT assessment classified 58 PSBs as 32 control and 26 case PSBs with bone fatigue (transverse fracture, focal osteolysis, or severe sclerosis). Opposing joint surfaces were also studied. PSB bone mineral density (BMD) was estimated. Results: Prevalence of fatigue injury in the PSB, condyle, and PSG was 44.8% (n=26), 43.1% (n=25), and 17.2% (n=10), respectively. For MC3 condyles with POD, 88.0% had fatigue injury in the corresponding PSB (OR = 53.2). Prevalence of PSB fatigue injury was 20.0% when there was PSG fatigue injury. The odds of a PSB having fatigue injury when the opposing MC3 PSG had signs of fatigue injury was 0.25. PSBs with opposing MC3 condyles containing a POD lesion had significantly increased BMD compared with opposing control condyles. BMD was significantly increased in PSBs with structural change associated with cyclic fatigue. Conclusions: Development of PSB fatigue and adaptive PSB sclerosis is associated with POD. Stress fractures in Thoroughbreds commonly affect the MCP joint. Condylar fractures occur from PSG or POD fatigue injury. PSB fractures are also common. Our findings suggest detailed clinical assessment of PSB structural change in racing Thoroughbreds diagnosed with POD is merited as part of routine injury prevention screening.

title: Structural damage of the cervical spinal cord within and beyond the maximal compression area in mucopolysaccharidosis types I and VI
abstract: BackgroundCervical spinal cord (CSC) compression and myelopathy are frequent, severe complications in mucopolysaccharidosis (MPS) types I and VI. Early detection is critical to prevent irreversible neurological deficits and preserve quality of life. This prospective study aimed to identify quantitative neuroimaging biomarkers of structural CSC damage and myelopathy in MPS I and VI. MethodsStructural and diffusion magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) of the CSC was analyzed in 17 MPS I patients, 3 MPS VI patients (19{+/-}7 years), and 19 case-matched healthy controls (20{+/-}7 years). CSC macrostructure (cross-sectional area, diameters) and microstructure (fractional anisotropy [FA], radial [RD], mean, axial diffusivities) were evaluated within and beyond the maximal compression areas. ResultsMPS patients demonstrated reduced CSC cross-sectional area and anterior-posterior diameter at upper cervical levels, alongside widespread microstructural alterations (lower FA, higher RD) throughout the CSC versus controls (pFDR<0.05). Restricted foramen magnum space was associated with microstructural damage at lower cervical levels without overt macrostructural compression. Morphological and microstructural metrics were sensitive to CSC compression and myelopathy severity (pFDR<0.05). Lower CSC integrity correlated with more advanced growth retardation (p<0.001). Among patients receiving hematopoietic stem cell transplantation, earlier treatment correlated with preserved upper CSC morphology (p<0.05). Distinct neuroimaging phenotypes were observed across MPS genotypes (pFDR<0.05). ConclusionsCSC MRI provides candidate neuroimaging biomarkers for early detection and characterization of myelopathy in MPS I and VI. Structural damage extends beyond primary maximal compression areas, highlighting these markers for clinical monitoring and future therapeutic trials.

title: AI-Enhanced Segmentation and Scoring of Histopathological Growth Patterns in Resected Colorectal Liver Metastases
abstract: Histopathological growth patterns, predominantly the presence of an encapsulated rim, serve as powerful prognostic biomarkers in colorectal liver metastases. However, conventional visual estimation is limited by interobserver variability, human rounding bias, and categorical thresholds. We aimed to develop and externally validate a deep-learning segmentation framework that produces continuous, spatially resolved, and objective encapsulation metrics from routine whole-slide images. In this multicenter study of chemo-naive resected CRLM patients, a modified nnU-Net architecture was developed on 40 pixel-annotated H&E-stained WSIs to segment liver parenchyma, tumor, and the encapsulation interface. Model performance was optimized across spatial resolutions. An automated continuous AI encapsulation score was computed to determine patient-level metrics. The prognostic value for 5-year overall survival was evaluated using restricted cubic spline Cox regression, a log-rank optimized threshold, and Kaplan–Meier survival analyses across a main cohort (Erasmus MC; n = 546, 1,910 WSIs) and an independent external validation cohort (Radboud UMC; n = 212, 615 WSIs). The segmentation network achieved optimal tissue boundary delineation at a resolution of 2.0 µm/pixel on the 40 annotated slides (overall foreground DICE: 0.86 ± 0.09; encapsulation DICE: 0.70 ± 0.11). Spline modeling demonstrated that while visual assessment displayed non-linear hazard plateaus, the continuous AI encapsulation score exhibited a linear reduction in mortality risk across the critical intermediate range (25%–75% encapsulation, p = 7.81 × 10 −4 ). Log-rank optimization identified a primary global threshold at 47.4% ( p = 3.73 × 10 −8 ), which in confirmed significant OS stratification in external validation ( p = 0.018). A secondary threshold was found at 69% ( p = 2.93 × 10 −6 ) that captured high-encapsulation favorable-risk patients matching the current manual 100% Rotterdam cut-off. Our deep-learning model transforms qualitative HGP grading into a continuous, explainable, and fully automated prognostic biometry. By eliminating observer subjectivity and capturing fine-grained risk gradients, the model establishes a scalable, standardized foundation for CRLM risk stratification on digital pathology.

title: Functional and Structural Neuroanatomic Correlates of Intraoperative Anesthetic Dose-Adjusted EEG Alpha Power Among Older Surgical Patients
abstract: Background: Alterations in intraoperative electroencephalography (EEG) alpha power and anesthetic dose-adjusted EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) have been associated with both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium (POD) among older surgical patients, yet the neurologic underpinnings of alterations in these anesthetic brain response patterns are unknown. Methods: We conducted a single center prospective observational cohort study (ALADDIN), of older adults undergoing non-cardiac/non-cranial surgery, which included preoperative structural and resting state functional MRI, lumbar punctures to obtain CSF, 32 channel intraoperative EEG recordings, and repeated POD assessments. To account for anesthetic dose, frontoparietal EEG alpha power (ADA-FP alpha power) was adjusted using our established formula: [intraoperative alpha power]/(2.5 - end-tidal MAC fraction). Multivoxel pattern analysis (MVPA) with follow-up seed-to-voxel analyses identified functional connectivity patterns associated with intraoperative ADA-FP alpha power. Voxel-wise regression analysis with threshold free cluster estimation (TFCE) correction was used to evaluate associations between cortical thickness and ADA-FP alpha power. CSF biomarker values were obtained from NULISA proximity extension assays. Delirium incidence and severity was assessed with the 3-Minute Diagnostic Confusion Assessment Method (3D-CAM). Delirium severity area under the curve (AUC) during hospitalization was defined as the sum of all 3D-CAM delirium severity scores within the postoperative hospitalization period (for up to 7 days after surgery). The Confusion Assessment Method for the Intensive Care Unit (CAM-ICU) was used in cases of non-verbal/intubated patients. Results: ALADDIN enrolled 215 patients, of whom 168 underwent surgery and had high-quality intraoperative EEG data (44.6% female; mean age 70.9 years). MVPA showed that ADA-FP alpha power was associated with altered functional connectivity within the bilateral frontal poles, left superior frontal gyrus and the right superior parietal lobule (p-FWE < 0.05). Seed-to-voxel analyses revealed that higher ADA-FP alpha power was associated with increased connectivity between DMN MVPA regions and DMN, DAN and salience/ventral attention and decreased connectivity with visual regions. Conversely, right superior parietal lobule connectivity shifted towards greater DMN segregation and increased somatosensory/motor coupling (p-FWE < 0.05). Lower ADA-FP alpha power was also associated with lower cortical thickness in left occipitotemporal and superior parietal cortices (TFCE-corrected p < 0.05). ADA-FP alpha power was also lower among participants with (vs those without) postoperative ward/floor delirium (mean difference, 1.33; 95% CI, 0.22 to 2.44; p=0.019), and ADA-FP alpha power was inversely associated with peak delirium severity (spearman's rho = -0.26; 95% CI, -0.40 to -0.11; p <0.001) and delirium severity AUC (spearman's rho = -0.28; 95% CI, -0.42 to -0.13; p < 0.001). Discussion: These findings suggest a functional and structural neuroanatomic basis for the decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power values seen among some older surgical patients, which may explain the association between decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and increased rates of both preoperative cognitive impairment and postoperative delirium. More specifically, these findings suggest that altered default mode and dorsal attention network connectivity is linked to decreased EEG ADA-FP alpha power and raise the possibility that preoperative/baseline functional connectivity alterations within these networks may play a role in delirium risk.

title: Fine-tuned Medical Vision-Language Model (MedGemma 1.5 4B) with and without Structured Radiologist Descriptors versus EU-TIRADS for Malignancy Risk Stratification of Thyroid Nodules at Ultrasound: A Tunisian Multicenter Diagnostic Accuracy Study
abstract: PurposeTo evaluate a medical vision-language foundation model fine-tuned on thyroid ultrasound images, with or without the radiologists structured descriptors, against expert-rated EU-TIRADS for the classification of thyroid nodules as benign or malignant. Materials and MethodsThis retrospective study included nodules that underwent ultrasound-guided fine-needle aspiration (FNA) between January 2019 and August 2025 in two Tunisian centers, with consecutive recruitment, together with a selection of images from an international public dataset. Of 1,580 nodules, 1,456 (272 malignant; 1,280 patients) with an interpretable cytological or histological reference standard were allocated at patient level to training (n = 942), validation (n = 258) and a test set sealed before training (n = 256; 51 malignant). MedGemma 1.5 4B was fine-tuned with low-rank adaptation under four input configurations: the image with nodule biometry, with or without age and sex (A, B); A with chain-of-thought supervision (C); and A plus the eleven qualitative descriptors of the radiologists structured report (D). The EU-TIRADS category was never a model input. Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLongs test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS [≥] 4 was the prespecified comparator, with [≥] 5 as a sensitivity analysis. ResultsConfig D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At [≥] 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Against EU-TIRADS [≥] 5 (sensitivity 92.2%, specificity 95.1%), Config D at its native threshold (88.2%, 94.1%) did not classify more nodules correctly (McNemar p = 0.22), and at its two other thresholds it classified fewer nodules correctly (p = 0.004 and 0.007). Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040. ConclusionGiven the ultrasound image together with the radiologists structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the [≥] 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation. Summary StatementA fine-tuned medical vision-language model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists structured report matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination of thyroid nodules and would have deferred most aspirations of benign category 4 nodules, at the cost of one or two missed category 4 cancers depending on the threshold, based on only three cancers in category 4. Key PointsO_LIOn a test set of 256 thyroid nodules sealed before training, the model given the ultrasound image and the radiologists 16-field structured report reached an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve of 0.953, non-inferior to expert EU-TIRADS (0.948). Areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROCs) were compared with DeLongs test and a prespecified non-inferiority margin of 0.05; EU-TIRADS [≥] 4 was the prespecified comparator, with [≥] 5 as a sensitivity analysis.

ResultsConfig D reached an AUROC of 0.953 (95% CI 0.909-0.976), versus 0.948 (0.894-0.972) for EU-TIRADS (difference +0.004, 95% CI -0.016 to +0.025), which met the non-inferiority criterion; Configs A-C, without the qualitative descriptors, reached 0.883-0.892 (Holm-adjusted p = 0.045 versus EU-TIRADS). At [≥] 4, EU-TIRADS had a sensitivity of 98.0% and produced 94 false positives among 205 benign nodules; at a threshold fixed on validation data, Config D reclassified 72 of them as negative while missing two additional cancers. Raw probabilities were miscalibrated (expected calibration error 0.117 for Config D), and Platt scaling within the test set reduced this error to 0.019-0.040.

ConclusionGiven the ultrasound image together with the radiologists structured descriptors, the fine-tuned model matched expert EU-TIRADS discrimination and, against the [≥] 4 threshold, reclassified most false positives as negative, a gain concentrated in category 4 and based on only three cancers in category 4. It is best positioned as a report-standardizing second reader in the EU-TIRADS 4 gray zone, pending prospective external validation.

title: Loss of Farnesoid X Receptor Signaling Promotes Choroidal Neovascularization in Mice
abstract: Choroidal neovascularization (CNV) is a defining feature of neovascular age-related macular degeneration (nAMD). Although anti-vascular endothelial growth factor (VEGF) therapies suppress neovascular activity, incomplete responses, recurrent leakage, and subretinal fibrosis remain important clinical challenges. The farnesoid X receptor (FXR) is a bile acid-activated nuclear receptor with anti-inflammatory, anti-fibrotic, and anti-angiogenic functions in other tissues, but its role in CNV is unknown. Analysis of publicly available human transcriptomic data (GSE135092) showed FXR expression in the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE)/choroid and significant downregulation in AMD-affected macular RPE/choroid. To define the role of FXR in CNV, laser photocoagulation was performed in wild-type (WT) and FXR-deficient (FXR-KO) mice, with disease progression assessed by in vivo imaging, histology, ex vivo choroidal sprouting, and endothelial cell assays. FXR expression in the RPE/choroid was reduced 14 days after laser injury. Compared with WT mice, FXR-KO mice developed larger CNV lesions, more extensive hyperfluorescence on fluorescein angiography, and increased lesion area during disease progression. FXR deficiency also impaired resolution of fibrotic remodeling. In WT mice, alpha-SMA peaked at day 14 and declined by day 21, whereas collagen I remained low throughout; in FXR-KO mice, both collagen I and alpha-SMA were significantly elevated relative to WT and remained significantly higher than WT at day 21. Consistent with these findings, FXR-deficient choroidal explants exhibited increased vascular sprouting, and FXR-KO endothelial cells formed more extensive capillary-like networks. Together, these findings identify FXR as an endogenous regulator of pathological angiogenesis, vascular leakage, mesenchymal activation, and fibrotic remodeling during CNV and provide a rationale for investigating FXR-directed strategies for nAMD.

title: Joint reconstruction of multi-contrast relaxation-diffusion imaging
abstract: ABSTRACT Diffusion MRI across multiple gradient directions, b-values and echo times (TEs) provides complementary tissue contrast but requires extensive sampling. Joint k-space and q-space undersampling requires reconstruction that preserves diffusion- and TE-dependent signal variation while exploiting shared anatomical information. Here we introduce DIFFUSE (Diffusion-relaxometry Implicit Field Fitting from Undersampled k – q Space across Echoes), a subject-specific joint k – q –TE image reconstruction framework. It fits a single implicit neural representation (INR) directly to complementary undersampled multi-coil k -space measurements across diffusion encodings and echo times. The INR (a self-supervised neural network) maps spatial location, b-value and TE to baseline b0 signals and spherical harmonic coefficients for directional diffusion-weighted image reconstruction. The measurement-specific forward model incorporates phase, coil sensitivities and motion and eddy current related transforms. We evaluated DIFFUSE using retrospective Human Connectome Project data, controlled motion simulations and in vivo multi-shell and multi-TE acquisitions. At sixfold in-plane acceleration, DIFFUSE reduced normalized mean squared error by 57–73% relative to SENSE across two diffusion shells in the retrospective experiment. In the controlled motion experiment, motion-aware DIFFUSE reduced normalized mean squared error by 66–72% relative to static DIFFUSE. The prospective study demonstrated multi-shell reconstruction at 1.3 mm isotropic resolution with significantly high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). In a separate multi-TE experiment, a single representation jointly reconstructed all nine contrasts corresponding to 3 b-value/TE combinations. DIFFUSE thus provides a common reconstruction strategy for accelerated protocols spanning multiple diffusion encodings and echo times.

title: NeCS-Flow: Necrosis-Guided Contrast-Enhanced MRI Synthesis with Rectified-Flow Refinement
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Gadolinium-based contrast agents raise concerns about tissue deposition, adverse reactions, and increased costs. Purpose To develop and validate a deep learning pipeline for gadolinium-free post-contrast T1w brain MRI synthesis incorporating necrotic scaling and Posterior-Mean Rectified Flow (PMRF) refinement, and to evaluate diagnostic utility through a blinded multi-reader study. Study Type Retrospective. Population 454 patients with adult-type gliomas (grade 2-4) from four publicly available datasets. Training used 374 patients; internal testing used 60 held-out patients; external validation used 20 patients. Field Strength/Sequence 1.5-3.0 T; pre-contrast T1w, T2w, and FLAIR as inputs; post-contrast T1w as synthesis target. Assessment A three-stage pipeline comprising nnU-Net Necrotic core segmentation, necrotic-scaling-guided U-Net Contrast Synthesis, and PMRF perceptual refinement (NeCS-Flow) was evaluated using whole-brain and tumor-region similarity metrics, enhancing tumor Dice scores, perceptual quality metrics, and a blinded three-reader study assessing diagnostic accuracy, enhancement detection, image quality, and real-versus-synthetic discriminability. Statistical Tests Paired t-tests and two one-sided tests for model comparison; Fisher’s exact test and two-sample t-tests for reader study comparisons, with p < 0.05 considered significant. Results Necrotic scaling consistently improved real versus synthetic enhancing tumor Dice internally (HGG: 0.793 to 0.816) and externally (HGG: 0.465 to 0.612). NeCS-Flow outperformed two benchmark architectures on all quantitative metrics in internal and external testing, although absolute enhancing tumor accuracy declined for all models on the external cohort. PMRF refinement improved perceptual realism across gliomas, reducing both FID and KID. Readers distinguished synthetic from real images only modestly above chance (overall accuracy 61.7%), and no significant differences between real and synthetic images were found for any clinical metric. Data Conclusion NeCS-Flow synthesizes perceptually realistic and diagnostically equivalent post-contrast T1w brain MRI, with necrotic scaling improving enhancing tumor delineation and PMRF refinement improving perceptual realism across gliomas. Performance on an external cohort was preserved relative to benchmark methods, though reduced in absolute terms.

title: Training-free generation of 4D CT and other rare acquisitions improves segmentation across modalities
abstract: RationaleRoutine clinical imaging captures anatomy under a limited set of physiologic and acquisition conditions, leaving segmentation models with sparse examples of how lesions and surrounding tissues deform with compression, respiration, or vascular pulsation. Standard image augmentation expands training datasets but does not explicitly model the mechanics underlying these changes. Patient-specific biomechanical simulation offers an approach to generate anatomically consistent images and corresponding segmentation masks under conditions absent from the original scan, without additional imaging or training a generative model. We hypothesized that incorporating this mechanistically grounded variability into training improves segmentation across imaging modalities. MethodsWe evaluate across three segmentation tasks: breast cancer on 3D digital breast tomosynthesis, lung tumors on chest CT, and carotid plaque on ultrasound. From each routine scan, patient-specific biomechanical models generate acquisitions absent from the original study--a range of breast compressions, the respiratory cycle, and arterial wall distension across the cardiac cycle. The resulting displacement fields deform both images and masks. Segmentation models were trained with and without the generated data across a range of standard image augmentation techniques, evaluated via cross-validation and held-out test sets. Realism was assessed through blinded reader studies, and generated respiratory motion was validated against real 4D CT. ResultsTraining on the generated acquisitions improved segmentation across modalities, increasing Dice scores by 6.6% for breast (p<0.05), 10.1% for lung (p<0.05), and 4.5% for carotid plaque (p>0.05) relative to the routine scans alone. Generated respiratory motion closely matched real gated 4D CT, with Dice of 0.94 {+/-} 0.02 for lung volume overlap. Blinded readers discriminated generated from real images at near chance (AUC: breast 0.61, lung 0.41, carotid 0.46). ConclusionsMechanistic simulation generates imaging acquisitions that clinical systems do not supply, without training data or additional scanning, and improves AI-based disease detection across modalities.

title: Explainable Multimodal AI for In-Hospital Detection of Lung Cancer and Heart Failure Using Routine Data: Development, Internal Validation, and Simulated Federated Evaluation
abstract: Objective: To determine whether combining four routine data sources improves in-hospital detection of lung cancer and heart failure, which sources drive each prediction, whether explanations are faithful, whether models are fair, and how much benefit federated training retains. Methods: In this retrospective single-centre study, we linked MIMIC-IV admissions (73,637 patients) to chest radiographs, radiology reports, 12-lead electrocardiograms (ECGs) and laboratory tests from the first 48 hours. For each disease, excluding prior cases, we compared single-source models, gradient boosting and early, late and attention-based fusion on patient-level splits. We tested explanations for faithfulness and weight dependence, audited performance by sex, age, race and ethnicity, and insurance, and simulated five unequal hospitals to compare federated, centralised and local training. Results: Lung cancer was coded in 1.7% and heart failure in 15.6% of patients. For lung cancer, attention fusion reached an area under the ROC curve (AUROC) of 0.833 (95% CI 0.809-0.859) against 0.753 for gradient boosting on laboratory data; for heart failure, 0.885 (0.878-0.892) against 0.794 (both p < 0.001). Early and late fusion performed similarly. Laboratory data and radiology reports contributed most to lung cancer, and the ECG to heart failure. Explanations passed a deletion test; a weight-randomisation check on absolute attributions passed for ECG but not for laboratory explanations. For heart failure, discrimination fell with age. Federated training recovered 95% of the centralised gain over local training for heart failure; for lung cancer, federated averaging (FedAvg) recovered 51% and FedProx 82%. Conclusion: Fusing routine data improved in-hospital detection of both diseases over laboratory data alone, and which data matter depends on the disease. Explanation checks should be run per source and per similarity measure, and performance in older patients monitored. For the rare outcome, FedProx, which limits drift between sites, retained more of the pooled benefit than FedAvg. External validation is needed.

title: Predicting HPV/p16 Status and Molecular Subtypes from Histopathology Slides using Deep Learning in Vulvar Squamous Cell Carcinoma
abstract: Vulvar squamous cell carcinoma (VSCC) comprises three prognostically distinct molecular subtypes: human papillomavirus (HPV)-associated, HPV-independent/p53-wildtype, and HPV-independent/p53-abnormal. Classification requires p16/p53 immunohistochemistry, which consumes tissue and is often incomplete in retrospective cohorts. We investigated whether deep learning could predict HPV/p16 status and molecular subtypes directly from routine hematoxylin and eosin–stained whole-slide images. Using features extracted with H-optimus-1, we developed two attention-based multiple-instance learning models: HERA, predicting HPV/p16 status, and HERMES, predicting the three molecular subtypes. Models were developed on 644 patients from three Dutch VSCC cohorts and tested on 286 patients from two independent cohorts. In independent testing, HERA achieved an area under the curve (AUC) of 0.84 (95% CI 0.75–0.91), with specificity 0.93, negative predictive value 0.94, and sensitivity 0.68. HERA-predicted groups reproduced the prognostic separation of HPV testing (log-rank p<0.001). HERMES achieved a macro-average AUC of 0.70 (0.66–0.75), with good discrimination for HPV-associated (0.80) but limited separation of HPV-independent/p53-abnormal (AUC 0.68) and HPV-independent/p53-wildtype (AUC 0.63). HERMES-predicted classes reproduced the prognostic hierarchy, with 5-year recurrence rates of 14.0% (HPV-associated), 31.1% (HPV-independent/p53-wildtype) and 43.3% (HPV-independent/p53-abnormal) (p=0.0051). Highly attended tiles showed basaloid cells and koilocytotic-like atypia in HPV-associated tumors, keratinizing nests with desmoplastic stroma in HPV-independent/p53-abnormal tumors, and well-differentiated keratinocytes with spongiosis in HPV-independent/p53-wildtype tumors. HERA could assign HPV/p16 status to large retrospective VSCC cohorts lacking ancillary testing, without consuming tissue, enabling HPV-stratified outcome analyses. Before such use, external validation of its discrimination and calibration across scanners and populations is required. HERMES suggests that molecular subtype information is encoded in hematoxylin and eosin–stained slides, but requires improved distinction between the HPV-independent subtypes.

title: Development and Validation of an Automated Image-Based Method for Prognostic Stratification in Lung Adenocarcinoma using Immunohistochemical Markers
abstract: ABSTRACT We present an automated image-based framework for quantifying biomarker expression in immunohistochemical (IHC) images and introduce the Marker Expression Level (MEL) score as an objective alternative to visual H-scoring. MEL addresses key limitations of existing automated methods by integrating tissue-region segmentation with tumour-area–weighted marker quantification, normalization to mitigate inter-sample and inter-batch staining variability, and robust quantification of nuclear, cytoplasmic, and membrane-associated biomarkers. The complete pipeline was developed as an open-source Fiji/ImageJ tool and is publicly available. We evaluated MEL using IHC images from 128 lung adenocarcinoma patients stained for BRCA1, GLUT1, and QKI, three markers forming a prognostic signature previously described by our group. Tissue regions were segmented using a machine learning-based Fiji plugin, and MEL scores were calculated within tumour regions. A normalization strategy accounted for inter-TMA staining variability. Agreement with visual H-scores was assessed using Spearman correlation. Prognostic performance was evaluated using Cox regression to derive a Combined Prognostic Index (CPI) incorporating MEL scores and tumour stage. Segmentation achieved high accuracy across tissue regions (Dice coefficients 0.69–0.99), with lower performance in highly immune-infiltrated stromal areas. MEL scores significantly correlated with visual H-scores for all markers (ρ = 0.61–0.69, p < 0.001). Normalization improved agreement for GLUT1 (ρ = 0.39 to 0.62). The derived CPI stratified patients into distinct risk groups with significant differences in disease-free and overall survival (p < 0.05), comparable to visual scoring. MEL provides a reproducible and scalable alternative to expert visual H-scoring and standard semi-automated approaches such as QuPath. Its integration with prognostic modelling reproduced a validated survival signature with performance comparable to expert scoring, supporting clinical and translational applicability. MEL is not a marginal refinement of existing digital scoring methods, but rather a clinically oriented and biologically adaptable framework designed to improve the robustness and reproducibility of automated IHC quantification.

title: Current gaps in downstream applications of fMRI foundation models: lessons learned from BrainLM & BrainHarmonix on Prevent-AD
abstract: Foundation models have driven major advancements in the language and vision domains, as seen in the popularity of Artificial Intelligence (AI) tools, and a growing number of studies are bringing the approach to human brain imaging. Whether these models are ready for independent researchers to use on clinical datasets has yet to be examined. We evaluated two recent fMRI foundation models, BrainLM and BrainHarmonix, on PreventAD, a dataset on adults with a family history of Alzheimers disease. We compared features from frozen and fine-tuned models against two baselines: functional connectivity and a dummy classifier that always predicts the most common class. The sample includes 343 subjects who passed quality control, with a subset of 218 who had amyloid PET imaging. We tested four prediction targets: sex, age, progression to mild cognitive impairment (MCI), and {beta}-amyloid burden. Both models required substantial changes to the released code. BrainLMs own data preparation workflow did not produce stable fine-tuning, which we achieved only after switching to a standard workflow implemented with the library Nilearn. BrainHarmonixs documentation did not specify how to normalize new data, so we resolved this by testing different alternatives. For sex, functional connectivity outperformed all foundation model features. For age group, the best foundation model feature, taken from BrainHarmonixs structural (T1-weighted) encoder, slightly exceeded functional connectivity, but the difference was not significant. For MCI and {beta}-amyloid, no feature exceeded the dummy classifier in accuracy, and the area under the curve (AUC) stayed near chance for all features. For both clinical targets, the most precise feature came from fine-tuned BrainLM, meaning a larger share of its positive predictions were correct than for functional connectivity, but neither difference reached statistical significance. These results suggested that the strong transfer to new tasks seen in large language models cannot yet be assumed for fMRI foundation models, and that both models required code adaptation that would preclude their streamlined adoption by independent groups. We recommend that future studies provide standardized data workflows and always report functional connectivity and dummy classifier baselines. For clinical targets with strong class imbalance, studies should report several metrics, including precision.

title: Feasibility study on using the diffusion-weighted imaging liver pulsation artifact as marker of liver fibrosis
abstract: BackgroundLiver diffusion-weighted imaging (DWI) often shows signal loss in the left lobe due to cardiac pulsation, known as the pulsation artifact. PurposeThis study was conducted to turn this bug into a feature. We hypothesized that the pulsation artifact, caused by mechanically transmitted waves, is influenced by tissue stiffness and, thereby, indicative of cirrhosis in the left liver lobe. Thus, we evaluated the potential of DWI pulsation artifacts to detect liver cirrhosis. Study typeThis study included both retrospective patients and prospective healthy volunteers. Study populationThirteen healthy volunteers, 16 patients with cirrhosis (Ishak 5 or 6), and three patients without cirrhosis (Ishak 0, 1, or 2) were included. Field Strength/SequenceImaging was performed at 1.5 T and 3 T using echoplanar DWI of the liver with two b-values, b50 = 50 s/mm{superscript 2} and b800 = 800 s/mm{superscript 2}. title: Quantized TotalSegmentator for Fast Abdominal Organ Segmentation on CPUs
abstract: BACKGROUNDTotalSegmentator is designed for a graphics processing unit (GPU), runs slowly on a central processing unit (CPU), and depends on Python, limiting CPU-only clinical deployment. OBJECTIVEThe purpose of this study was to evaluate whether TS-Portable, a self-contained CPU executable running 8-bit integer (INT8)-quantized TotalSegmentator models, is noninferior to the reference implementation across 15 abdominal organs in an external multicenter cohort, quantify CPU-only runtime, and demonstrate spleen volumetry on a picture archiving and communication system (PACS) reading station. METHODSThis retrospective study compared TS-Portable with the reference Python implementation on 100 external multicenter CT scans and 28 chronic liver disease series. Per-case mean Dice similarity coefficient (DSC) and 3-mm normalized surface distance (NSD@3 mm) across 15 organs (1.5-mm resolution) and spleen-only mode were tested against a 0.01 noninferiority margin (paired bootstrap 95% CIs). Workstation and PACS runtimes were recorded; spleen volumes were compared via Lins concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) and Bland-Altman analysis. RESULTSThe external cohort included 100 patients (53 men, 47 women; mean age, 53 {+/-} 16 [SD] years). Across 15 organs, TS-Portable was noninferior for mean DSC (difference, 0.00017; 95% CI, 0.00003-0.00031; p < .001) and NSD@3 mm (difference, 0.00015; 95% CI, -0.00002 to 0.00031; p < .001) and in spleen-only mode (both p < .001). Workstation 1.5-mm median runtime was 48.0 seconds for TS-Portable on CPU versus 342.5 seconds on CPU (ratio, 7.14) and 61.5 seconds on GPU (ratio, 1.28) for the reference. On PACS, CPU spleen volumetry took 5.8 versus 43.4 seconds, agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.9999; bias, 0.2%; 95% limits of agreement, -7.2% to 7.6%) and manual contours (CCC, 0.989; bias, -6.8%). In 28 chronic liver disease series, TS-Portable ran from DICOM in 6.5 seconds (median), agreeing with the reference (CCC, 0.99999) and manual contours (CCC, 0.992; bias, -3.4%). CONCLUSIONTS-Portable achieved noninferior abdominal organ segmentation accuracy compared with the reference implementation while running faster on a workstation CPU than the reference on a GPU. CLINICAL IMPACTSelf-contained deployment enables fast multiorgan segmentation on CPU-only computers and spleen volumetry within seconds on a standard reading station, without dedicated GPUs or software installation. HighlightsO_ST_ABSKey FindingC_ST_ABSAcross 100 external multicenter CT examinations, a quantized, self-contained CPU executable of TotalSegmentator was noninferior to the reference implementation for 15-organ segmentation accuracy and 7.14-fold faster on a workstation CPU, and completed reading-station spleen volumetry in a median of 5.8 seconds. ImportanceCompiling and quantizing three-dimensional segmentation models into a standalone CPU executable removes GPU and software-installation barriers, enabling rapid quantitative CT analysis on standard clinical workstations.

title: Quantifying Localized Tumor-Infiltrating Lymphocytes by Deep Learning on H&E Images: Analytical Validation and Prognostic Value in Lung Adenocarcinoma
abstract: Tumor-infiltrating lymphocytes (TILs) are a critical determinant of response to immune checkpoint inhibitor (ICI) therapy in lung adenocarcinoma (LUAD). However, assessing the clinical utility of TIL quantification is challenging due to subjective manual scoring and differences in methodology, including some that may obscure localized immune responses critical to ICI response. Together, these issues limit our understanding of potential prognostic benefits of performing routine TIL quantification. Here, we present the “focal TIL score,” an artificial intelligence-powered biomarker derived from routinely generated Hematoxylin & Eosin (H&E) pathology images which measures TIL density within tiles across the entire relevant tissue region in order to account for spatial heterogeneity of localized lymphocytic infiltration. Underlying this method are two deep learning models that ensure accurate, reproducible, and interpretable quantification: one for lymphocyte detection trained on IHC-derived ground truth, and one for segmentation of tumor and tumor-adjacent stroma region (“scorable region”) trained on consensus pathologist annotations. We performed an analytical validation of the two models, demonstrating high overall performance: lymphocyte model concordance correlation coefficient (CCC) = 0.90, scorable region model Dice score = 0.87. We then performed a prognostic association study in a cohort of 685 ICI-treated LUAD patients and saw that, the focal TIL score was significantly associated with overall survival (HR=0.60, 95% CI 0.48-0.75, P<0.001), outperforming the standard biomarker PD-L1. Our findings show that quantifying the spatial intensity of immune infiltration, rather than the global average, provides a superior measure of the anti-tumor immune response. The accessibility and standardization associated with this approach may enable further studies and developments in precision oncology for LUAD.

title: Real-World Effectiveness of Osteoporosis Treatments on Bone Strength and the Impact of Sequential Anabolic Therapy
abstract: Summary In this real-world biomechanical CT analysis study, romosozumab showed greater increases in vertebral bone strength and density than teriparatide and denosumab in treatment-naïve women with postmenopausal osteoporosis. Romosozumab also increased bone strength after prior teriparatide, whereas twice-weekly teriparatide failed to maintain gains achieved with prior romosozumab. Purpose Evidence regarding the comparative effectiveness of osteoporosis treatments in improving bone strength in clinical practice remains limited. This real-world study compared the effectiveness of different osteoporosis treatments in women with postmenopausal osteoporosis (PMO), including treatment-naïve patients initiating Romo, TPTD, or DMAb (Study 1) and patients switching from one anabolic therapy to another (Study 2). Methods Japanese women with PMO aged >55 years were included. In Study 1, 57, 34, and 50 women received Romo, TPTD, or DMAb, respectively, for 12 months. In Study 2, 16 received Romo for 12 months after TPTD (TPTD-Romo) and 29 received twice-weekly TPTD for 12 months after Romo (Romo-TPTD). The primary and secondary endpoints were average percent change from baseline at 12 months in vertebral bone strength and volumetric BMD (vBMD), respectively, assessed using biomechanical CT analysis (BCT). Results At baseline, overall bone strength and vBMD were comparable across groups in both studies. In Study 1, average percent change (95% CI) in vertebral strength was highest with Romo (39.5% [34.2, 44.7]), followed by TPTD (24.4% [18.8, 30.0]), and DMAb (10.9% [7.6, 14.2]). In Study 2, vertebral strength increased by 16.1% (10.6, 21.6) with TPTD-Romo, and decreased by 7.7% ( 10.7, 4.6) with Romo-TPTD despite subsequent TPTD treatment. Similar trends were observed for vertebral vBMD. Conclusion In this real-world BCT study, Romo showed greater increases in both vertebral bone strength and density versus TPTD and DMAb in treatment-naïve women with PMO. Among prior TPTD, Romo further increased bone strength and density; however, twice-weekly TPTD failed to maintain the gains following prior Romo.

title: Motion-robust high-resolution 3D-GRASE pseudo-continuous ASL perfusion imaging at 3T
abstract: PurposeHigh resolution arterial spin labeling (ASL)-based perfusion imaging is desirable for many applications but suffers from low SNR and motion sensitivity due to the necessity for highly segmented readouts. Acquisition and reconstruction strategies were optimized for motionrobust high-resolution pseudo-continuous arterial spin labeling (pCASL) of the brain at 3T using segmented 3D Gradient and Spin Echo (3D-GRASE) at 2.0-mm isotropic resolution. MethodsA high-resolution 3D-GRASE pCASL sequence was implemented at 3T and evaluated with a focus on the interaction between background suppression strength and motion-corrected reconstruction, together with the fat suppression and control-tag subtraction strategies that strong suppression requires. Motion correction was performed using a novel motion-compensated (alignedSENSE-based) reconstruction that simultaneously estimates the motion and image, accounting for contrast changes between tag and control data. Eight healthy volunteers were scanned under motion-free and cued motion conditions. Image quality was assessed against motion-free reference images using peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and a structural similarity index measure (SSIM). ResultsThe optimized acquisition-reconstruction pipeline enabled robust 2.0-mm isotropic pCASL at 3T and showed improved resistance to motion-related degradation. Strong BGS provided near-complete suppression of static tissue, and water excitation reduced lipid contamination and improved coil sensitivity estimation. The regularized alignedSENSE motion correction further improved perfusion-image quality, increasing SSIM by 18.7% under Strong BGS. ConclusionRobust high-resolution pCASL at 3T can be achieved through combined optimization of acquisition and reconstruction. The combination of Strong BGS, water excitation, reference-superimposed processing, and regularized motion correction mitigates motion-related degradation and yields higher-quality perfusion images for high-resolution ASL.

title: Revealing multiscale architecture of the intact human spine using hierarchical phase-contrast tomography
abstract: Background CT and MRI provide detailed clinical assessment of the human spine; however, their millimeter-scale spatial resolution limits direct visualization of tissue microarchitecture and interfaces. Hierarchical phase-contrast tomography (HiP-CT) enables ex vivo non-destructive, micron-resolution imaging of intact human organs without exogenous contrast agents, extending anatomical assessment to spatial scales inaccessible to conventional clinical imaging. Purpose To evaluate the capability of HiP-CT to visualize macro- to microanatomy of an intact adult human spine ex vivo . Materials and Methods An intact spine (C1-L5) from a 62-year-old male donor without known skeletal disease was formalin-fixed and imaged by HiP-CT at the European Synchrotron. Whole-spine imaging was performed using 16.26 µm isotropic voxels, with selected regions of interest imaged using 2.2 µm voxels. Ex vivo MRI was performed for anatomical comparison. Three-dimensional segmentation and quantitative analyses included intervertebral disc (IVD) grading, annulus fibrosus fiber tracing, and vertebral trabecular micro-morphometry. Results HiP-CT enabled high spatial-resolution, multiscale imaging of the intact human spine, simultaneously visualizing vertebral bone and endplate, IVDs, spinal cord and meninges, nerve roots and ganglia, vasculature, ligaments, and musculature. Three-dimensional segmentation and virtual sectioning mapped neurovascular anatomy and vertebral vascular supply, without exogenous contrast enhancement, while preserving their relationships with surrounding tissues. Whole-spine images enabled quantitative analysis of annulus fibrosus fiber organization and vertebral trabecular microarchitecture, permitting the detection of focal posterolateral fiber disruption at the L4-L5 IVD and regional differences in trabecular architecture between cervical and lumbar vertebral bodies. Local tomography resolved annulus fibrosus lamellae, vertebral endplate Haversian systems, and facet joint hyaline cartilage at micron resolution. Conclusions HiP-CT enables non-destructive, multiscale three-dimensional imaging of the intact human spine while preserving tissue relationships across spatial scales and tissue boundaries. HiP-CT images could provide an ex vivo microanatomical reference for future correlation with clinical imaging investigations of spinal disease and in the discovery and validation of imaging biomarkers. Key results Synchrotron-based hierarchical phase-contrast tomography enables non-destructive, multiscale three-dimensional imaging of an intact adult human spine using 16.26 µm isotropic voxels, resolving both mineralized and non-mineralized tissue. Local tomography using 2.2 µm isotropic voxels reveals additional microstructural detail without exogenous contrast agents or sectioning. Whole-spine imaging enables quantitative characterization of intervertebral disc fiber architecture and vertebral trabecular morphometry, alongside visualization of neurovascular anatomy while preserving spatial relationships across the intact specimen. Summary statement Hierarchical phase-contrast tomography enables non-destructive multiscale imaging of the intact human spine, resolving microarchitecture across tissues and interfaces and providing a basis for bridging clinical imaging with underlying three-dimensional microanatomy.

title: Toward Electrical Impedance Tomography of Functional Activity in the Retina
abstract: Electrical Impedance Tomography (EIT) is a non-invasive electrical imaging technique that reconstructs spatial variations in tissue conductivity. Traditionally used for thoracic imaging, EIT has recently been extended to neural applications in the brain and peripheral nerves. This study investigates the feasibility of using EIT to image functional neural activity in the retina. We present computational modeling of EIT measurements for image reconstruction of small conductivity perturbations across different layers of the ex-vivo mouse retina with electrodes placed in epiretinal configuration. Experimentally, we describe the design of a multi-electrode array suitable for impedance measurements under these conditions and report preliminary recordings of light-evoked impedance changes in response to wide-field optical retinal stimulation. Our computational results suggest that small conductivity perturbations of 200µm diameter and 5% conductivity variation are experimentally detectable by high-end biopotential recording equipment and could be localized by EIT imaging within ≈13% of inter-electrode distance and ≈22% of retinal thickness, respectively. In preliminary recordings, we observed slow impedance variations of 13.0±9.3 µV (0.37±0.44%) in response to retina-wide light pulse trains, when performing impedance measurements with 10 µA applied current at 2-8 kHz. These variations were characterized by a slow time course, distinct from the fast neural EIT signals associated with action potentials, and may reflect extracellular or metabolic processes linked to retinal activation. Our modelling and technical results support the feasibility of retinal EIT, while the experimental observations are preliminary and motivate further controlled studies. Retinal EIT could significantly advance retinal electrophysiology research and prosthetic development.

title: Tumor Associated Neutrophils Extend NETs To Spatially Drive Necroptosis In Glioblastoma
abstract: Background Glioblastoma is pathologically characterized by extensive pseudopalisading necrosis, a hallmark linked to therapeutic resistance and dismal prognosis. While traditionally viewed as a passive ischemic event, the precise radiogenomic drivers and spatial immune architectures orchestrating active tumor necrosis remain poorly understood. Methods We integrated macroscopic clinical MRI radiomics with public genomic datasets (n=3,639), single-cell spatial transcriptomics, and high-resolution protein immunofluorescence (IF) assays in a novel co-mutant murine model to map the necrotic microenvironment. Results Radiomic analysis of patient MRIs demonstrated that high tumoral necrotic volume serves as a powerful independent biomarker for poor long-term survival. This macro-structural necrosis phenotype is radiogenomically driven by cell-intrinsic TP53 , PTEN , and NF1 (PPN) co-mutations. Spatial transcriptomic profiling of PPN-deficient tumors revealed distinct cellular topography, separating a proliferative, invasive niche (EGFR + SOX + , Type Inv ) from a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche (ERBB3 + , Type Nec ). Mechanistically, Type Nec cells deploy a prominent CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine milieu that actively recruits and prompts tumor-associated neutrophils to undergo neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) formation. This overactive neutrophil infiltrate drives a feed-forward loop of intrinsic tumor necroptosis mediated by the release of the damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) protein HMGB2. This cascade could be therapeutically dismantled using targeted anti-inflammatory compounds. Finally, multi-cohort clinical validation confirmed that an HMGB2 high signature dictates a high-risk, myeloid-rich immunosuppressive microenvironment in glioblastoma patients. Conclusions Our findings redefine glioblastoma necrosis as an active, mutation-driven immunopathological process. The HMGB2-mediated DAMP necroptosis cascade and associated myeloid chemokines provide robust prognostic biomarkers and immediate therapeutic vulnerabilities to disrupt the immunosuppressive necrotic niche. Key Points Clinical Stratification via Radiomics: Preoperative MRI analysis of 1,079 glioblastoma patients establishes a necrotic core volume threshold of 18.57% as a robust, non-invasive biomarker for early survival divergence and dismal long-term prognosis. Genomic Orchestration of Necrosis: Cross-species modeling identifies a high-risk somatic PPN co-mutation profile yielding two topographically distinct niches: an invasive niche EGFR + SOX + , Type Inv ) from a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche (ERBB3 + , Type Nec ). Vascular Loop and DAMP Cascade: TypeNec cells deploy a CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine milieu driving perivascular neutrophil recruitment and MPO + CitH3 + NETosis, sparking a feed-forward loop of hypoxia and necrosis driven by tumor-derived HMGB2 high that is pharmacologically targetable. Online Key Points (85 characters) Preoperative MRI biomarker of necrotic threshold determines long-term prognosis. Cross-species co-mutation profile yielding distinct invasive and necrotic niches. N eutrophil extracellular traps spark DAMP-targetable feed-forward necroptosis loop. Importance of the Study Tumor necrosis is a hallmark diagnostic feature of glioblastoma, historically characterized as a passive consequence of local tissue ischemia. This study redefines glioblastoma necrosis as an active, genetically driven immunopathological process. By integrating macroscopic clinical MRI radiomics from over 1,000 patients with single-cell spatial transcriptomics and a novel co-mutant mouse model, we reveal that cell-intrinsic TP53 , PTEN , and NF1 co-mutations actively dictate a hyper-aggressive necrotic niche. Mechanistically, these mutated tumor cells deploy a CCL5/CXCL2 chemokine cascade to recruit neutrophils, triggering an overactive neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) and a HMGB2-mediated damage-associated molecular pattern (DAMP) loop that accelerates tissue destruction and myeloid immunosuppression. Crucially, we demonstrate that this pathogenic axis can be tracked non-invasively via standard neuroimaging and pharmacologically dismantled with anti-inflammatory small molecules, providing immediate diagnostic stratifications and a brand-new therapeutic vulnerability to disrupt the glioblastoma microenvironment. Lay Summary Dead tissue zones inside glioblastoma brain tumors, known as necrosis, are tied to poor patient survival. While long believed to be an accidental result of rapid tumor growth cutting off oxygen, this study reveals that tumor cells actively trigger this cell death. Driven by specific genetic mutations, these cells release distress signals that recruit immune cells called neutrophils. These neutrophils create a destructive, inflammatory loop that worsens the disease. Glioblastoma is pathologically characterized by extensive pseudopalisading necrosis, a hallmark linked to therapeutic resistance and dismal prognosis. While traditionally viewed as a passive ischemic event, the precise radiogenomic drivers and spatial immune architectures orchestrating active tumor necrosis remain poorly understood.

Methods

We integrated macroscopic clinical MRI radiomics with public genomic datasets (n=3,639), single-cell spatial transcriptomics, and high-resolution protein immunofluorescence (IF) assays in a novel co-mutant murine model to map the necrotic microenvironment.

This cascade could be therapeutically dismantled using targeted anti-inflammatory compounds. Finally, multi-cohort clinical validation confirmed that an HMGB2 high signature dictates a high-risk, myeloid-rich immunosuppressive microenvironment in glioblastoma patients.

Our findings redefine glioblastoma necrosis as an active, mutation-driven immunopathological process. The HMGB2-mediated DAMP necroptosis cascade and associated myeloid chemokines provide robust prognostic biomarkers and immediate therapeutic vulnerabilities to disrupt the immunosuppressive necrotic niche.

title: Robot-Assisted Transcranial Magnetic Stimulation Guided by Cortical Topography
abstract: Transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) is widely used for functional brain mapping and neuromodulation, but conventional neuronavigation systems typically rely on simplified volumetric brain models that do not fully capture subject-specific cortical geometry. We developed and evaluated a novel cortical-topography-guided framework for improving TMS planning, coil alignment, and stimulation reliability. The framework integrates an enhanced head-MRI co-registration strategy based on the iterative closest point (ICP) algorithm using a three-dimensional cortical mesh reconstructed from structural MRI. This approach was designed to improve neuronavigation by more accurately aligning the participant’s head with the MRI-derived cortical anatomy, thereby reducing co-registration error. Robot-assisted TMS (RA-TMS) was used to preserve the planned coil pose relative to cortical targets. Registration accuracy, coil alignment error, and motor-evoked potential (MEP) responses at the hand area of the primary motor cortex (M1) were evaluated and compared between RA-TMS and conventional manual TMS approach, which did not consistently preserve cortical topography-guided stimulation. ICP-based co-registration reduced the registration error between the head and MRI model from 5.83 ± 1.04 mm to 1.07 ± 0.03 mm. Compared with manual alignment, RA-TMS reduced translational error from 14.79 ± 8.03 mm to 5.22 ± 1.68 mm and rotational error from 7.01 ° ± 2.29 ° to 1.09 ° ± 0.33 ° ( p < 0.001). RA-TMS also produced larger and more consistent MEP responses than manual TMS (0.27 ± 0.05 mV vs. 0.03 ± 0.01 mV, p < 0.001). Incorporating cortical topography-guided planning, combined with refined co-registration and robotic stabilization, improves coil alignment accuracy and the reliability of stimulation outcomes.

title: HELIOS: A spatial omics-informed multi-organ cell atlas enables AI-based tumour microenvironment profiling and biomarker discovery from routine histopathology
abstract: Spatial omics defines tumour microenvironments with high biological resolution but remains difficult to scale across large clinical cohorts. We developed HELIOS (H&E Learning Informed by Omics and Spatial Profiling), which transfers spatial-omics-derived cell identities into routine haematoxylin and eosin histology for interpretable single-cell tumour microenvironment profiling. HELIOS integrates 12.9 million cells from 60 specimens across 13 tissue types and four spatial profiling platforms, spanning eight epithelial, immune, stromal, and vascular populations. The resulting multiclass detector generalised across independent histopathology benchmarks. Applied to colorectal, breast, and lung cancers, HELIOS recapitulated molecular subtype-associated microenvironment states and identified prognostic immune and stromal phenotypes. Tumour-infiltrating lymphocytes were consistently associated with favourable outcomes, whereas neutrophil and fibroblast phenotypes showed cancer-specific associations. HELIOS-derived features remained prognostic after adjustment for clinicopathological and molecular variables. These findings demonstrate that spatial omics can provide scalable biological supervision for extracting clinically relevant tumour microenvironment features from routine H&E, supporting scalable risk stratification and biomarker development across clinical cohorts and retrospective pathology archives.

title: Routine Chest CTA Reliably Quantifies Left Ventricular Myocardial Mass
abstract: ABSTRACT Background Routine chest computed tomography angiography (CTA) is the primary imaging modality for thoracic aortic disease, yet cardiac information within these examinations remains underutilized. We evaluated whether left ventricular myocardial mass (LVMM) can be reliably quantified from routine non–electrocardiographically (ECG)-gated chest CTA and its application in thoracic aortic pathology. Methods CTA scans were obtained from 257 patients without aortic disease and 181 patients with thoracic aortic aneurysm or dissection. LVMM was quantified using automated three-dimensional segmentation. In a separate 10-patient validation cohort, LVMM was compared across end-systolic, end-diastolic, and non-ECG-gated source reconstructions. CTA-derived LVMM was compared with published echocardiographic and cardiovascular magnetic resonance (CMR) reference values using Cohen’s d. Results LVMM remained stable across cardiac phases and non-ECG-gated images (mean coefficient of variation, 2.4%), whereas left ventricular volume varied substantially (36.9%). CTA-derived LVMM demonstrated small effect sizes with the Penn method ( d = 0.22) and moderate effect sizes with ASE linear ( d = 0.67), area-length ( d = 0.68), and CMR ( d = 0.63). LVMM increased through young adulthood, with minimal association with age beyond 30 years. LVMM was comparable between patients with thoracic aneurysms and normal adults (140 ± 43 g vs. 141 ± 40 g; adjusted p = 1.0) but significantly greater in acute (199 ± 61 g) and chronic (191 ± 57 g) aortic dissection (both adjusted p < 0.001). Conclusions Routine non-ECG-gated chest CTA enables reliable automated LVMM quantification without additional imaging or radiation and may facilitate large-scale investigations of ventricular remodeling in thoracic aortic disease.

title: Distinct Biomarker Signatures of CMR-Defined Myocardial Remodeling in Moderate Aortic Stenosis
abstract: Background Moderate aortic stenosis (AS) is associated with adverse outcomes, yet the myocardial response to pressure overload varies substantially between patients and is incompletely reflected by valve hemodynamics. We aimed to determine whether circulating biomarkers of myocardial stress, injury, and fibrosis associate with cardiac magnetic resonance (CMR)-defined myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Methods Eighty-nine patients with moderate AS prospectively underwent CMR (cine imaging, T1 mapping, extracellular volume fraction [ECV], late gadolinium enhancement [LGE]) with concurrent measurement of NT-proBNP, high-sensitivity troponin T, sST2, TIMP-1, and Galectin-3. Biomarker associations with the phenotype-defining CMR parameters were tested with adjustment for age, sex, and renal function and correction for multiple testing, and patients were additionally classified into 4 hierarchical remodeling phenotypes. Results Six of 20 biomarker-CMR associations remained significant after correction for multiple testing. NT-proBNP tracked LV mass index (beta=0.50), ECV (beta=0.35), and LGE burden (beta=0.43, all q<0.05). TIMP-1 and Galectin-3 were selectively associated with native T1 (both beta=0.35, q=0.012), and sST2 was inversely associated with LV mass index (beta=-0.27, q=0.046). TIMP-1 (adjusted OR 2.18 per SD, 95% CI 1.37-3.48, q=0.005) and NT-proBNP (OR 2.10, 1.19-3.69, q=0.026) increased with higher hierarchical remodeling phenotype. No biomarker was associated with echocardiographic mean gradient, peak velocity, or indexed valve area after correction. Conclusions Circulating biomarkers showed distinct associations with CMR measures of myocardial remodeling in moderate AS. Matrix-related biomarkers were associated with native T1, whereas NT-proBNP was associated across several remodeling domains. These signals were not measurably related to valve hemodynamics. Registration URL: https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05851209 . Unique identifier: NCT05851209 . Clinical Perspective What Is New? In patients with moderate aortic stenosis, myocardial remodeling on cardiac magnetic resonance was heterogeneous, and circulating biomarkers showed distinct associations with individual remodeling domains. The matrix-related biomarkers TIMP-1 and Galectin-3 were associated with native T1, whereas NT-proBNP was associated with several remodeling domains. What Are the Clinical Implications? No biomarker was associated with echocardiographic stenosis severity, suggesting that circulating biomarkers may add information on the myocardium that valve hemodynamics do not capture. If validated in larger cohorts, matrix-related biomarkers such as TIMP-1 could help select patients with moderate aortic stenosis for advanced myocardial tissue characterization.

title: Study protocol for a prospective multicenter longitudinal cohort study on progression of moderate aortic valve stenosis — the MODAS Study
abstract: Background Calcific aortic stenosis (AS) is one of the most common and prognostically relevant valvular heart diseases, with a growing global burden driven by population ageing. Prediction of disease progression from moderate to severe AS, which would be instrumental for earlier diagnosis and treatment, remains challenging. At the same time, moderate AS is increasingly recognized as a heterogeneous condition associated with clinically relevant risk, particularly in patients with cardiac damage, heart failure, or rapid disease progression. Conventional echocardiographic parameters incompletely capture the biological heterogeneity underlying AS progression. The MODAS study was established to investigate biomarkers and mechanisms of AS progression and outcome using longitudinal multimodal phenotyping. Methods The MODAS Study is a prospective, multicenter, longitudinal observational cohort study enrolling adults with moderate calcific tricuspid AS at three tertiary heart valve centers in Germany. Participants undergo standardized baseline assessment including clinical phenotyping, laboratory testing, electrocardiography, transthoracic echocardiography, cardiac computed tomography and cardiac magnetic resonance imaging. Biospecimens are collected for biomarker, immunologic, proteomic, and genetic analyses, including genome-wide association studies and assessment of clonal haematopoiesis. Participants are followed annually for up to 5 years with repeat clinical assessment, laboratory testing, and echocardiography. The primary endpoint is time to progression to severe AS according to 2025 ESC/EACTS guideline criteria or aortic valve replacement for severe AS, adjudicated by the local multidisciplinary Heart Team. Secondary endpoints include all-cause mortality and additional clinical outcome trajectories. Multimodal data integration will be used to develop and validate prediction models for disease progression and outcome. Discussion The MODAS Study will provide a harmonized, deeply phenotyped longitudinal dataset to improve risk stratification in moderate AS and to identify imaging, inflammatory, and genetic markers associated with rapid progression and adverse outcomes. The study is designed to support future personalized surveillance strategies, improved selection for earlier intervention, and mechanistic understanding of calcific AS progression. Trial registration ClinicalTrials.gov NCT05851209 . Registered on 9 May 2023.

title: Biopsy-Validated Deep Learning Mapping of Glioma Infiltration Beyond Contrast Enhancement Using Multiparametric MRI
abstract: BackgroundGlioblastoma (GBM) exhibits diffuse tumor infiltration beyond contrast-enhancing margins into FLAIR-hyperintense brain tissue, where infiltrative tumor is not visible on conventional MRI. We developed and validated the infiltrative Tumor Burden (iTB) map, a deep learning biomarker that uses multiparametric MRI (mpMRI) to identify infiltrative tumor within these non-enhancing regions. MethodsPreoperative mpMRI datasets from 80 patients with WHO grade II-IV gliomas and 24 patients with brain metastases were retrospectively analyzed. Imaging included pre- and post-contrast T1-weighted, T2-weighted, FLAIR, dynamic susceptibility contrast perfusion and diffusion MRI-derived maps (rCBV, rCBF, ADC). Spatially localized stereotactic biopsies from non-enhancing glioma regions provided histopathologic ground truth while peritumoral brain metastasis regions served as biologically grounded non-tumor controls. A 3D convolutional neural network was trained on voxel-centered mpMRI patches using patient-level cross-validation and an independent test set, with data augmentation optimized using a greedy local search strategy. ResultsModel development included 121 biopsy-localized samples from 56 glioma patients and 104 non-tumor samples from 26 brain metastasis patients. Augmentation optimization significantly improved independent test-set performance, increasing accuracy from 74.5% to 85.5% and AUC from 0.859 to 0.942 (p = 0.008). Ensemble-derived voxel-wise iTB maps demonstrated low infiltration probabilities in brain metastases and extensive regions of elevated infiltration probability in glioblastoma, consistent with expected biology. ConclusionsThe iTB biomarker generates voxel-wise maps of tumor infiltration within non-enhancing FLAIR abnormalities. Validated against image-localized histopathology and independent testing, it achieved high diagnostic performance and may improve surgical planning, radiotherapy targeting, and assessment of glioma burden.

title: Linking clinical border morphology to cell-scale growth mechanisms in melanoma: a segmentation-to-simulation alignment study
abstract: An irregular border is among the most informative visual cues for melanoma, yet the prevailing quantitative treatment of that irregularity, the box-counting fractal dimension, has rarely been connected to the cell-scale mechanism that produces it. We measured seven boundary descriptors on 1,581 lesions from the 2018 International Skin Imaging Collaboration archive segmented by an automatic thresholding route, retaining the expert ground-truth route as a sensitivity arm, and compared their medians across benign, in situ, and invasive grades. We then built a hybrid cellular automaton and swept four canonical cell-level mechanisms, scoring every simulated boundary with the same measurement code used on the patient images, before testing two mechanisms that lift the empty-neighbour division rule and aligning them to the observed malignant signature with a variance-based sensitivity analysis. The malignant signature is lobulation, not roughness: compactness rises from 1.351 to 1.810, solidity falls from 0.910 to 0.853, and convexity falls from 0.936 to 0.839 from benign to invasive lesions, with areas under the curve near 0.74, while the fractal dimension varies by only 0.024 across the three grades. All four canonical mechanisms, including loss of contact inhibition, converge on near-circular clusters at a distance of 1.147 to 1.166 from the malignant target. A long-range spatial heterogeneity in the growth rate, by contrast, reproduces the observed signature to a distance of 0.187, with the correlation length of the field, not its amplitude, the dominant parameter by total-effect index. A smooth, long-range growth-rate field is therefore sufficient to generate the lobular borders that characterise invasive melanoma, whereas the empty-neighbour assumption common to cellular automata is not. Because the winning field is imposed rather than emergent, the study resolves the alignment between border morphology and cell-scale mechanism while leaving open how such heterogeneity could arise from cell-autonomous dynamics. Author Summary Melanoma is the deadliest form of skin cancer, and clinicians have long used the raggedness of a lesion’s edge as a warning sign. Computer methods usually summarise that raggedness with a single number, the fractal dimension, which measures how much fine detail a border contains. We tested that habit on 1,581 skin lesions and found it misleading. What distinguishes malignant from benign lesions here is not fine roughness but a handful of large lobes: the outline bulges and dents at a coarse scale rather than fraying at a fine one. We then asked what kind of cell behaviour could build such a border. We grew virtual tumours using simple rules for cell division, movement, and crowding, and we measured their edges with exactly the same code we applied to the patient images. The usual suspects, namely cells that ignore crowding, migrate further, or vary in their growth, all produced smooth and round tumours. Only when we let the growth rate vary smoothly across the tumour did the simulated edge acquire the observed lobes. We could impose that variation but cannot yet explain where it comes from, and we say so. That open question is our next target.

title: Estimating glioblastoma migration-to-proliferation ratio from single time-point MRI data via radial density distribution
abstract: Glioblastoma (GBM) tumors with a high migration-to-proliferation ratio (D/k) are associated with treatment resistance, motivating the estimation of D/k from routine pre-treatment magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data and the investigation of mechanisms underlying its heterogeneity across patients. Unlike previous approaches based on nested spherical approximations of enhancing and non-enhancing tumor volumes, we incorporate the spatial arrangement of the enhancing and non-enhancing tumor regions by deriving a 1D tumor density distribution from their segmentations and fitting a 1D reaction-diffusion model to estimate D/k. We achieved an error of under 5% when comparing our method to synthetic density distributions and found excellent correlation with synthetic tumor segmentations (Pearson correlation coefficient (PCC) = 0.996). We then evaluated associations between patient-specific D/k values and their clinical, transcriptomic, and radiomic features. When applied to 102 pre-treatment MRI scans from the Brain Tumor Segmentation (BraTS) 2017 dataset, elevated D/k significantly correlated with reduced overall survival (log-rank p = 0.01), older age (p = 0.04), and a trend toward lower Karnofsky Performance Status (p = 0.059). In a subset of 91 patients with available microarray data, mesenchymal-like phenotypes consistently exhibited elevated D/k across three established molecular subtype classifications (p = 0.013, p = 0.055, and p = 0.127). Elastic Net regularization followed by overrepresentation analysis revealed an enrichment of glycosylation-related pathways among genes associated with D/k variability (p = 0.0123 and p = 0.0368). Furthermore, Multi-Omic Factor Analysis identified a radiomic factor correlated with D/k (r = 0.57, p = 4×10-9), with the highest-weighted features corresponding to smoothness of the non-enhancing tumor region on T2 and FLAIR.
